Google, Microsoft, and Amazon have to justify the AI spending boom this week

No summary available

Google (GOOG, GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), and Amazon (AMZN) have one big, collective task on their digital shoulders this week as they report their quarterly earnings: They need to justify the AI spending boom. The stakes are high — these companies lead a week of corporate results that account for mo...

Google (GOOG, GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), and Amazon (AMZN) have one big, collective task on their digital shoulders this week as they report their quarterly earnings: They need to justify the AI spending boom. The stakes are high — these companies lead a week of corporate results that account for more than a third of the S&P 500's (^GSPC) earnings Like Meta (META) before them, the biggest question they'll face is likely about AI spending. Specifically, what that number is and how it compares to the expected returns. "All eyes will be on AI monetization vs. spending, with hyperscalers' 2027 capex estimates already revised up by nearly 90% YTD," Bank of America strategist Savita Subramanian wrote in a note on Tuesday. Tech execs having to justify their huge AI spending has been a feature of earnings reports for the past two years. Skeptical investors are eager to see returns on investment, and Wall Street has been rattled by cycles of doubt. But conditions in the economy and the investing environments have changed, heightening the urgency to show results. The recent tech sell-off has thrown AI financing into the spotlight. Companies leading the data center build-out have flagged. And investors have expressed mixed feelings about tech giants like Meta selling shares and borrowing to finance their AI ambitions. The massive demand for financing has increased the competition for capital. That has put pressure on tech companies to preemptively raise enormous sums of money, especially as Wall Street prepares to shepherd the blockbuster IPOs of two frontier AI labs — Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) as soon as next month and OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) likely next year. AI business dynamics are also changing. The era of tokenmaxxing is officially over. Businesses are becoming pickier and choosier with their AI spending — scaling back, using less expensive models, and experimenting with different services. The slowdown in token spending among corporations suggests the lavish appetite for compute only existed when it was effectively free. And so, if the demand for compute isn't infinite and is actually price-sensitive, that means justifying AI costs will be more important. Lastly, Meta's Muse and the early success of personal assistant AI agents have scrambled product priorities. Meta has reoriented the entire company around the division behind Muse and envisions its operations becoming a massive service network and revenue engine. The cash might not come now or even soon, but it will flow, the bull thesis goes. Zuckerberg might have a mixed record, but his company is behind him. And he had the benefit of moving first. The other tech giants this week will have to come up with answers too. Follow Hamza Shaban on X @hshaban.

Microsoft to report Q1 earnings with Wall Street looking for further Azure growth

No summary available

Microsoft (MSFT) will report its first quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, providing the market with a better view of demand for AI apps and services. The announcement comes just two days after Microsoft said it is offering buyouts to upward of 60,000 eligible employees as it seeks to red...

Microsoft (MSFT) will report its first quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, providing the market with a better view of demand for AI apps and services. The announcement comes just two days after Microsoft said it is offering buyouts to upward of 60,000 eligible employees as it seeks to reduce expenses amid its massive AI build-out. Q1 also marks the first time Microsoft will report earnings under its new segment structure. The company announced the change in Q4, saying that rather than Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing, it will switch to two segments: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. Microsoft's Agents and Infra segment will garner the most attention and include the company's Azure, Microsoft 365 cloud services, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions, and frontier and support services. Microsoft stock drifted lower before the bell on Wednesday, ahead of its earnings release. Devices and Consumer will include Microsoft's search and advertising businesses, Xbox, and Windows OEM and devices. Microsoft's stock was a laggard for most of fiscal 2026 but picked up following the company's Q4 earnings, climbing about 35% since July. Investors following the company's Q1 report will be on the lookout for more information about Azure and Copilot growth as Microsoft continues to push its AI services. For the quarter, Wall Street is anticipating earnings per share of $4.27 on revenue of $90.6 billion, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus estimates. That would be an improvement from the EPS of $4.13 and revenue of $77.6 billion the company saw in the same period last year. Agents and Infra revenue is expected to climb 22.5% to $75.6 billion, with Azure and Microsoft 365 bringing in $32.2 billion and $27.4 billion, respectively. Devices and Consumer sales are projected to decline 6% to $15 billion. Capital expenditures, including leases, are anticipated to top $45.9 billion in the quarter, up from the $19.3 billion Microsoft spent in Q1 last year. Remaining performance obligations (RPO) are expected to come in at $705.6 billion, up 77% from the $389 billion reported in fiscal Q1 2026. RPOs are contracts that Microsoft has booked with customers but hasn't yet received revenue for. Email Daniel Howley at dhowley@yahoofinance.com. Follow him on Twitter at @DanielHowley. Verisk Brings Its Proprietary Insurance Intelligence to Amazon and Microsoft AI Platforms, Expands Offerings Within Claude

New integrations with Amazon Quick and Microsoft Copilot, along with expanded offerings within Claude by Anthropic, bring trusted underwriting, premium audit and weather intelligence into insurers' preferred AI workflows JERSEY CITY, N.J, Oct. 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Verisk (Nasdaq: VRSK), a s...

New integrations with Amazon Quick and Microsoft Copilot, along with expanded offerings within Claude by Anthropic, bring trusted underwriting, premium audit and weather intelligence into insurers' preferred AI workflows JERSEY CITY, N.J, Oct. 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Verisk (Nasdaq: VRSK), a strategic data analytics and technology partner to the global insurance industry, today announced new integrations with Amazon Quick and Microsoft Copilot, along with expanded offerings within Claude by Anthropic, providing insurers with additional ways to access Verisk's proprietary insurance intelligence across enterprise AI platforms. The expansion broadens controlled, permissioned access to Verisk's trusted insurance intelligence, increasing the information and resources available to insurers. The new integrations build on the launch of Verisk Underwriting Intelligence in Claude earlier this year, expanding the ways authorized insurers can access Verisk underwriting, premium audit and property-level weather information through natural-language interactions in the AI environments they already use. Verisk's goal is simple: make trusted insurance information easier for insurers to find and apply, reducing research time and helping insurance professionals make informed decisions more efficiently, leaving them more time to serve policyholders and customers. New capabilities include: Amazon Quick integration with access to ISO® Loss Costs and Premium Audit Advisory Service (PAAS®) content for eligible customers. Microsoft Copilot integration with access to ISO Loss Costs and PAAS content for eligible customers. Claude by Anthropic: Expansion of Verisk Underwriting Intelligence within Claude to include PAAS resources alongside ISO Loss Costs, as well as a new Verisk Benchmark® connector providing controlled, permissioned access to property-level hail and wind history. "In an increasingly complex risk environment, underwriting and claims performance increasingly depends on precision, trusted intelligence and the responsible application of AI," said Saurabh Khemka, president of Verisk Underwriting Solutions. "AI is most valuable when it helps insurance professionals get relevant, reliable information when they need it. By making that information easier to access and apply, we're helping insurance professionals work more efficiently while maintaining the rigor and confidence they need to act on that information." "AI is changing how insurance professionals work, and how they interact with and draw value from the information they rely on," said Steven Kauderer, president of Verisk Claims Solutions. "Our focus is on helping clients navigate these changes, making the insurance knowledge they need more immediate and useful so they can better serve policyholders as the industry continues to evolve."

In this article, we will summarize the bulls' thesis on AMZN. Amazon.com, Inc.'s share was trading at $253.10 as of October 27th 2026. AMZN's trailing and forward P/E were 20.04 and 23.10 respectively according to Yahoo Finance. This isn't the first time we see a technology company pitched as a great investment. AMZN shares gained 9.90% over the last 12 months. Comparable stocks like Alphabet gained 16.76% during the same period. Gil C / Shutterstock.com In July, we published an article about the 12 Best Dow Stocks to Invest In Right Now and AMZN ranked 1st in that article. Before getting into our analysis, let's take a look at the business and why some investors like the stock so much. Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) operates one of the largest consumer, cloud computing, advertising, and logistics ecosystems in the world. Its investment case increasingly depends on AWS, artificial intelligence infrastructure, advertising, and a shift toward higher-margin businesses rather than traditional e-commerce. Sales growth has been strong and steady, rising 12% in 2024 and an estimated 15% in 2025, with a similar pace expected in 2026 as Amazon.com, Inc. moves toward $1 trillion in annual revenue. The stock trades around 21 times earnings at $262 per share, a multiple that rises closer to 30 times once one-time, non-operating gains are stripped out — a reminder that investors are really paying for future AWS growth, AI monetization, and margin improvement rather than today's reported earnings. The bullish case rests on several growth engines reinforcing one another. Higher-margin segments such as AWS, advertising, third-party seller services, and subscriptions are letting profits grow faster than overall sales. Online retail is still the biggest source of revenue for Amazon.com, Inc., but advertising and third-party services are more profitable, while AWS remains both the company's main earnings driver and its gateway into the AI boom. As more companies increase spending on AI infrastructure, AWS stands to benefit from rising demand for computing power, storage, databases, and AI tools such as Amazon Bedrock, opening up a fresh growth cycle for the business.

When former Microsoft product manager Mike Kostersitz was suddenly laid off last year after 31 years at the company, he was in total shock. "Me and 120 other anonymous faces got told our jobs had been eliminated," he told Business Insider. "After 31 years, you would expect at least your manager or your VP or somebody to come to you and say, 'Hey Mike, this is going to happen and here is why.'" Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP The mass layoff was part of a company-wide focus on "reducing management layers and streamlining processes," a Microsoft spokesperson told Business Insider. And it looks as though they're not finished cutting costs just yet. The company recently announced it'll be offering voluntary buyouts to select employees for the second time this year. Roughly 60,000 employees in select departments and seniority levels will be offered different severance packages that coincide with their individual employee standing. The move is meant to reconfigure the company's workforce to better support AI initiatives. While a buyout gives you the choice to stay or go, many U.S. workers don't have the same option, and are simply forced out — like Kostersitz. But even if a worker chooses to accept a buyout, they'll need to find more work when the money runs dry. Microsoft's layoffs and buyouts are part of a larger trend. In recent months, Amazon and Meta have trimmed their workforces. Amazon cut additional jobs in May after cutting 14,000 jobs in October 2025, citing a shift toward AI automation. As of January, it plans to cut 16,000 roles total. Meta has eliminated hundreds of roles this year and is expected to reach thousands. Cost-cutting and AI are the top reasons employers are using to explain the job reductions. Overall, the tech industry has announced over 195,000 job cuts in 2026. Despite this, U.S. unemployment remains relatively low and has slightly decreased since the start of the year. It would appear, though, AI is the competitive edge many job seekers need on their resume going forward. South Korea fines Google, Apple for pushing app developers onto their payment systems

No summary available

South Korea's media and telecommunications regulator on Wednesday ordered Google and Apple to pay a combined 63.7 billion won (€42.7m) accusing them of exploiting their grip on app stores to push developers towards their own payment tools and of stalling app reviews. The two US companies have faced...

South Korea's media and telecommunications regulator on Wednesday ordered Google and Apple to pay a combined 63.7 billion won (€42.7m) accusing them of exploiting their grip on app stores to push developers towards their own payment tools and of stalling app reviews. The two US companies have faced similar penalties elsewhere, including in the EU. The Korea Media and Communications Commission (KMCC) fined Google 42.9 billion won (€28.7m) and Apple 20.8 billion won (€13.9m) after an investigation that began back in August 2022. It found that both firms had broken a 2021 law that stops app store operators from making developers use a specific payment system, a rule that South Korea was the first country in the world to put into force. On paper, Google and Apple allowed developers to offer other payment systems inside their apps. However, they charged a 26% commission on those payments, only slightly below the 30% they charge for their own systems, and held back some features, which the commission said left developers with little real choice. Payments through external websites were also blocked altogether. The regulator also found that the companies held up app reviews without properly explaining the reasons to developers, or saying when the reviews would restart. Apple was also found to have charged South Korean developers more than those elsewhere between 2015 and January 2023, as it calculated its commission on prices that included value-added tax. Both companies must now let South Korean developers place links to outside payment options in their apps and improve how they review apps. They have one month to submit plans and three months to make the changes. Commission chair Kim Jong-cheol said he hoped the sanctions would bring real change to the market, reiterating that South Korean law would be applied equally to domestic and foreign companies. Google and Apple have not yet reacted publicly to the decision. The case echoes battles in the EU, where the Digital Markets Act (DMA), a law setting rules for the biggest online platforms, prohibits so-called gatekeepers from stopping developers directing users to cheaper deals. In April 2025, Apple was fined €500 million by the European Commission under the DMA for blocking such steering on its app store, a decision it has appealed. In August this year, following what it called close collaboration with the Commission, Apple announced new EU terms taking effect on 1 October. They cut its standard commission on in-app purchases to 26% from 30% and set a 15% rate when developers send users elsewhere to complete a purchase.

Alphabet's (GOOGL) Google and Apple (AAPL) were fined 42.9 billion won ($32 million) and 20.81 billion won, respectively, by the Korea Media and Communications Commission for practices prohibited under the Telecommunications Business Act, including forcing app developers to use specific in-app payment systems, the regulator said Wednesday. Inspections and investigations launched in 2022 found app market operators conducted prohibited practices, including forcing specific payment methods, unfairly delaying app reviews and, in Apple's case, impairing users' interests, the regulator said. Both companies charged a 26% commission for the use of third-party payment methods while limiting access to features available through their own payment services, effectively forcing developers to use only their own in-app payments, the regulator said. Apple was also found to have imposed discriminatory commissions on domestic and overseas app developers between July 2015 and January 2023, the commission said. The commission said it also issued corrective orders requiring both companies to revise the terms and conditions of their contracts with app developers. South Korea fines Google and Apple over unfair app market practices

No summary available

SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — South Korea on Wednesday fined Alphabet's Google and Apple a combined 63.7 billion won ($47.6 million), saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews. The Korea Media ...

SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — South Korea on Wednesday fined Alphabet's Google and Apple a combined 63.7 billion won ($47.6 million), saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews. The Korea Media and Communications Commission, the country's media and telecommunications regulator, spent years investigating the U.S. tech giants for allegedly violating a 2021 law that prohibits app store operators from forcing developers to use specific payment systems. The commission fined Google 42.9 billion won ($32 million) and Apple 20.8 billion won ($15.5 million) and ordered both companies to let South Korean developers use external payment links within their apps and to improve their app review procedures. In a statement to The Associated Press, Apple said it "respectfully" disagrees with the decision, arguing that its current practices comply with South Korean law and that it is evaluating its legal options. Apple said its in-app payment system allows users to make secure transactions while protecting them from predatory tactics and fraud and that such safeguards that could potentially be lost when paying through alternative methods. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The commission said Google and Apple unfairly pushed app developers toward their own in-app payment systems while barring payments through external websites. Although the companies technically allowed third-party payment systems within apps, they charged developers a 26% commission and withheld some features available through their own systems, effectively forcing developers to use only their in-app payment systems, the commission said. The commission said it also found instances where the companies delayed app reviews without clearly explaining to developers the reasons for the delays or when reviews would resume. It also accused Apple of charging South Korean developers higher commissions than developers elsewhere from 2015 to January 2023. South Korea has for years closely scrutinized the business practices of foreign technology companies operating in its market. In 2021, it became the first country to enforce a law prohibiting app market operators such as Google and Apple from requiring users to use their own in-app payment systems.

YouTube was the first free platform to break in. It turned creator videos into something people actually sit down and watch. Paid streamers have spent the years since raising prices to keep up. Now another giant wants the same spot in your living room. Instagram, owned by Meta Platforms (META), now has an app for Apple (AAPL) TV, MacRumors reported. Apple TV is the last stop in a steady expansion: December 2025: Testing began on Amazon (AMZN) Fire TV in the U.S. February 2026: The app reached Google TV devices from Alphabet (GOOGL) June 2026: Samsung smart TVs were added, along with plans for longer videos, episodic series and live broadcasts October 2026: Apple TV support arrived Meta has been blunt about the reason. This maker of iPhones, iPads and other products has an established record of topping earnings estimates, especially when looking at the previous two reports. The company boasts an average surprise for the past two quarters of 3.14%. For the most recent quarter, Apple was expected to post earnings of $1.88 per share, but it reported $1.91 per share instead, representing a surprise of 1.60%. For the previous quarter, the consensus estimate was $1.92 per share, while it actually produced $2.01 per share, a surprise of 4.69%. Thanks in part to this history, there has been a favorable change in earnings estimates for Apple lately. In fact, the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction) for the stock is positive, which is a great indicator of an earnings beat, particularly when combined with its solid Zacks Rank. Our research shows that stocks with the combination of a positive Earnings ESP and a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) or better produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time. In other words, if you have 10 stocks with this combination, the number of stocks that beat the consensus estimate could be as high as seven. The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a version of the Zacks Consensus whose definition is related to change. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier. Apple has an Earnings ESP of +0.69% at the moment, suggesting that analysts have grown bullish on its near-term earnings potential. When you combine this positive Earnings ESP with the stock's Zacks Rank #3 (Hold), it shows that another beat is possibly around the corner. The company's next earnings report is expected to be released on November 2, 2026. Investors should note, however, that a negative Earnings ESP reading is not indicative of an earnings miss, but a negative value does reduce the predictive power of this metric. Many companies end up beating the consensus EPS estimate, but that may not be the sole basis for their stocks moving higher. On the other hand, some stocks may hold their ground even if they end up missing the consensus estimate.

Google (GOOG, GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), and Amazon (AMZN) have one big, collective task on their digital shoulders this week as they report their quarterly earnings: They need to justify the AI spending boom. The stakes are high — these companies lead a week of corporate results that account for more than a third of the S&P 500's (^GSPC) earnings Like Meta (META) before them, the biggest question they'll face is likely about AI spending. Specifically, what that number is and how it compares to the expected returns. "All eyes will be on AI monetization vs. spending, with hyperscalers' 2027 capex estimates already revised up by nearly 90% YTD," Bank of America strategist Savita Subramanian wrote in a note on Tuesday. Tech execs having to justify their huge AI spending has been a feature of earnings reports for the past two years. Skeptical investors are eager to see returns on investment, and Wall Street has been rattled by cycles of doubt. But conditions in the economy and the investing environments have changed, heightening the urgency to show results. The recent tech sell-off has thrown AI financing into the spotlight. Companies leading the data center build-out have flagged. And investors have expressed mixed feelings about tech giants like Meta selling shares and borrowing to finance their AI ambitions. The massive demand for financing has increased the competition for capital. That has put pressure on tech companies to preemptively raise enormous sums of money, especially as Wall Street prepares to shepherd the blockbuster IPOs of two frontier AI labs — Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) as soon as next month and OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) likely next year. AI business dynamics are also changing. The era of tokenmaxxing is officially over. Businesses are becoming pickier and choosier with their AI spending — scaling back, using less expensive models, and experimenting with different services. The slowdown in token spending among corporations suggests the lavish appetite for compute only existed when it was effectively free. And so, if the demand for compute isn't infinite and is actually price-sensitive, that means justifying AI costs will be more important. Lastly, Meta's Muse and the early success of personal assistant AI agents have scrambled product priorities. Meta has reoriented the entire company around the division behind Muse and envisions its operations becoming a massive service network and revenue engine. The cash might not come now or even soon, but it will flow, the bull thesis goes. Zuckerberg might have a mixed record, but his company is behind him. And he had the benefit of moving first. The other tech giants this week will have to come up with answers too. Follow Hamza Shaban on X @hshaban.

A Connecticut man is headed to prison after pleading guilty to defrauding Amazon out of millions of dollars in an elaborate logistics scheme. Ameer Nasir was sentenced to two years in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release for the crime, in which he defrauded Amazon out of more than $3.5 million. He remains out on a $300,000 bond and will report to prison on Nov. 12. Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP Nasir pleaded guilty to wire fraud on March 6 after being arrested on May 8, 2025. The wire fraud charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. He has also been ordered to pay restitution to Amazon of $3,547,090.93. Nasir targeted Amazon Logistics via a service called Amazon Relay, which connects trucking companies to transportation assignments. He registered 23 trucking businesses with the retailer's subsidiary, which organizes the transport of trailers between cities, warehouses and fulfillment centers. According to the Department of Justice, one of those accounts was created in the name of Nasir's business, Pak Express Transport. The others were created under false names or by fraudulently using the names of other trucking and transportation companies. From December 2019 through February 2021, officials say Nasir used these accounts to sign up for over 1,000 transportation assignments with Amazon Logistics. He manipulated data in the company's transportation management system to give the impression he had completed trailer movements when he had not, virtually checking trailers in and out of the system. He then submitted fraudulent invoices to Amazon Logistics, which were paid. For example, drivers must now verify their identities and trailer telematics keep track of shipments that are in transit. Trailers included GPS technology when Nasir was running his scheme, but he reportedly evaded it by using a manual override to make it appear he had completed the trailer movements.

Amazon orders coders to rein in AI use as costs mount

No summary available

Amazon has ordered its coders to rein in their AI use amid concerns that tech workers are blowing through company budgets on chatbots. The online retailer told staff that technology giants' efforts to track AI usage by their software engineers were "deeply flawed" and risked driving up costs. Some...

Amazon has ordered its coders to rein in their AI use amid concerns that tech workers are blowing through company budgets on chatbots. The online retailer told staff that technology giants' efforts to track AI usage by their software engineers were "deeply flawed" and risked driving up costs. Some technology businesses have started ranking staff by how many AI tokens, the building blocks of AI bots, they use. It has driven a trend of "tokenmaxxing" among workers as they compete to maximise their AI use. However, bosses have since had to curb usage and limit AI spending after engineers burned through budgets on coding projects. In a note to the company's coders, Terk Terkowitz, an Amazon vice president, said companies that tried to track AI adoption by ranking staff on token use risked driving up costs. He said: "We know that using these metrics could, if used as a target instead of a measure, drive negative outcomes, increasing costs (tokenmaxxing is at odds with frugality) and increasing complexity." The warning comes as technology giants grapple with surging AI costs while employees race to incorporate the new technology into their work. Earlier this year, Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard tracking the most prolific AI users, measured by how much they spent on AI. The trend has raised concerns that staff have been doing needless tasks to boost their rankings while racking up substantial computing costs. Disney and Meta have adopted similar leaderboards, prompting the Facebook owner to implement AI token caps for some employees to keep costs under control. While Amazon has not implemented a cap on AI tokens, it has urged software engineers to consider the benefits the technology brings. It said: "Judgment and care are key ... we believe that it is best to measure and be measured by long-term outcomes." Amazon insisted that AI would be at the centre of software engineering. However, it told staff not to use the technology if they did not need it. The company said: "If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing." Under Andy Jassy, Amazon's chief executive, the company has been ramping up its internal use of AI. Mr Jassy has previously said the company would need fewer employees in the future as more work became automated. Amazon is a major backer of Anthropic, the developer of Claude. Amazon has invested $13bn (£10bn) in the AI company, which is now valued at $190bn, putting it in line for a major windfall when Anthropic goes public next month. New integrations with Amazon Quick and Microsoft Copilot, along with expanded offerings within Claude by Anthropic, bring trusted underwriting, premium audit and weather intelligence into insurers' preferred AI workflows JERSEY CITY, N.J, Oct. 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Verisk (Nasdaq: VRSK), a strategic data analytics and technology partner to the global insurance industry, today announced new integrations with Amazon Quick and Microsoft Copilot, along with expanded offerings within Claude by Anthropic, providing insurers with additional ways to access Verisk's proprietary insurance intelligence across enterprise AI platforms. The expansion broadens controlled, permissioned access to Verisk's trusted insurance intelligence, increasing the information and resources available to insurers. The new integrations build on the launch of Verisk Underwriting Intelligence in Claude earlier this year, expanding the ways authorized insurers can access Verisk underwriting, premium audit and property-level weather information through natural-language interactions in the AI environments they already use. Verisk's goal is simple: make trusted insurance information easier for insurers to find and apply, reducing research time and helping insurance professionals make informed decisions more efficiently, leaving them more time to serve policyholders and customers. New capabilities include: Amazon Quick integration with access to ISO® Loss Costs and Premium Audit Advisory Service (PAAS®) content for eligible customers. Microsoft Copilot integration with access to ISO Loss Costs and PAAS content for eligible customers. Claude by Anthropic: Expansion of Verisk Underwriting Intelligence within Claude to include PAAS resources alongside ISO Loss Costs, as well as a new Verisk Benchmark® connector providing controlled, permissioned access to property-level hail and wind history. "In an increasingly complex risk environment, underwriting and claims performance increasingly depends on precision, trusted intelligence and the responsible application of AI," said Saurabh Khemka, president of Verisk Underwriting Solutions. "AI is most valuable when it helps insurance professionals get relevant, reliable information when they need it. By making that information easier to access and apply, we're helping insurance professionals work more efficiently while maintaining the rigor and confidence they need to act on that information." "AI is changing how insurance professionals work, and how they interact with and draw value from the information they rely on," said Steven Kauderer, president of Verisk Claims Solutions. "Our focus is on helping clients navigate these changes, making the insurance knowledge they need more immediate and useful so they can better serve policyholders as the industry continues to evolve."

The deal includes 25 megahertz of mobile-satellite spectrum key to Amazon's satellite-to-phone plans. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the acquisition would bring "even more competition, coverage, and capacity." AST holds authorization for up to 248 satellites and has partnerships with AT&T, Verizon and FirstNet. Shares of AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) slipped over 1% in overnight trading late Tuesday as the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) cleared Amazon's $11.5 billion Globalstar acquisition, pushing the tech giant's satellite-to-phone ambitions forward and setting the stage for tougher competition. ASTS stock jumped 6% on Tuesday to $41.96, but shares are still down 29% for the month. See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox The FCC's Space Bureau approved the transaction on Tuesday, including the transfer of 25 megahertz of Globalstar's internationally harmonized mobile-satellite spectrum. "This will enhance Amazon's offering of direct-to-device (D2D) services, which will mean even more competition, coverage, and capacity," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said on X. The deal will pair Amazon Leo's satellite-building capabilities, launch arrangements and ground infrastructure with Globalstar's existing network and spectrum. The spectrum is key to Amazon's satellite-to-phone ambitions. In its approval order, the FCC said Amazon has applied to operate a global direct-to-device system but would lack the mobile-satellite spectrum needed to run it without the acquisition. Amazon plans to use Globalstar's assets to expand capacity and bring more services to areas beyond cellular coverage. The FCC said the deal could help close coverage gaps, boost emergency communications and improve data services for businesses and industrial users. "By approving this deal, the FCC has empowered Amazon Leo to deliver fast, next-gen satellite broadband services, increase competition, and help communities stay connected all across the country," Carr said in the announcement. The FCC's review also highlights how the deal could strengthen a rival to AST SpaceMobile. In its approval order, the agency cited arguments from Public Knowledge and New America's Open Technology Institute that combining Amazon's resources with Globalstar's assets could create a stronger competitor to SpaceX and T-Mobile's satellite offering, as well as AST's partnership with AT&T. The order also notes AST's ties with Verizon and FirstNet.

VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more

No summary available

Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public. Stakes held by firms including Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures, and Spark Capital are expected to return billions. Yet according to Anthropic's S-1, none of those VC firms owns 5%, the threshold for being included in the principal ...

Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public. Stakes held by firms including Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures, and Spark Capital are expected to return billions. Yet according to Anthropic's S-1, none of those VC firms owns 5%, the threshold for being included in the principal stockholders' table. That's highly unusual. In a typical tech IPO, lead venture investors hold double-digit-percentage stakes in the startups they backed. The reason is Anthropic's size. At its $965 billion private valuation, a 1% stake is worth nearly $10 billion, so, for example, Menlo's roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5% of the company, according to recently reported Bloomberg figures. While the venture firms may lack sizable percentage stakes, Anthropic sold large stakes to strategic partners, companies that are also its business partners. Indeed, Amazon is likely the single largest financial beneficiary of the IPO. Amazon first backed Anthropic in 2023 with a commitment to invest up to $4 billion in the AI company. Since then, Amazon has poured billions more into Anthropic. Instead of taking stock upfront, Amazon structured much of its investment as convertible notes, a type of debt that converts into shares upon an IPO or sale. According to the S-1, Amazon holds convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal outstanding as of June 30. That is Anthropic's entire debt load. But as Anthropic's valuation soared across successive funding rounds, the shares those notes will convert into became far more valuable. Amazon's own filings valued its note holdings at $97.9 billion as of June 30. As the value of Amazon's convertible notes surged, Anthropic had to record the growing value of what it owes on its books. It reported the adjustments on its income statement under "change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs," a line that totaled $72.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The charge is non-cash, meaning no money left the company. Amazon's notes could convert into as many as 1.84 billion shares, according to the S-1. But a cap limits Amazon to 12% of Anthropic's "partially diluted" share count, a figure that counts some shares not yet issued, such as stock options. Amazon can waive the cap. Notes that can't convert will stay outstanding and convert in later quarters, subject to the same limit. But the notes are only part of Amazon's holdings. It further invested $10 billion in nonvoting preferred stock (a type of equity), in the second quarter, according to Amazon's quarterly report for the period ended June 30. Amazon did this by investing $5 billion in each of Anthropic's last two funding rounds. Combined with the $8 billion it invested in the notes from 2023 through 2025, that brings Amazon's total investment to about $18 billion.

South Korea fines Google, Apple for pushing app developers onto their payment systems

No summary available

South Korea's media and telecommunications regulator on Wednesday ordered Google and Apple to pay a combined 63.7 billion won (€42.7m) accusing them of exploiting their grip on app stores to push developers towards their own payment tools and of stalling app reviews. The two US companies have faced...

South Korea's media and telecommunications regulator on Wednesday ordered Google and Apple to pay a combined 63.7 billion won (€42.7m) accusing them of exploiting their grip on app stores to push developers towards their own payment tools and of stalling app reviews. The two US companies have faced similar penalties elsewhere, including in the EU. The Korea Media and Communications Commission (KMCC) fined Google 42.9 billion won (€28.7m) and Apple 20.8 billion won (€13.9m) after an investigation that began back in August 2022. It found that both firms had broken a 2021 law that stops app store operators from making developers use a specific payment system, a rule that South Korea was the first country in the world to put into force. On paper, Google and Apple allowed developers to offer other payment systems inside their apps. However, they charged a 26% commission on those payments, only slightly below the 30% they charge for their own systems, and held back some features, which the commission said left developers with little real choice. Payments through external websites were also blocked altogether. The regulator also found that the companies held up app reviews without properly explaining the reasons to developers, or saying when the reviews would restart. Apple was also found to have charged South Korean developers more than those elsewhere between 2015 and January 2023, as it calculated its commission on prices that included value-added tax. Both companies must now let South Korean developers place links to outside payment options in their apps and improve how they review apps. They have one month to submit plans and three months to make the changes. Commission chair Kim Jong-cheol said he hoped the sanctions would bring real change to the market, reiterating that South Korean law would be applied equally to domestic and foreign companies. Google and Apple have not yet reacted publicly to the decision. The case echoes battles in the EU, where the Digital Markets Act (DMA), a law setting rules for the biggest online platforms, prohibits so-called gatekeepers from stopping developers directing users to cheaper deals. In April 2025, Apple was fined €500 million by the European Commission under the DMA for blocking such steering on its app store, a decision it has appealed. In August this year, following what it called close collaboration with the Commission, Apple announced new EU terms taking effect on 1 October. They cut its standard commission on in-app purchases to 26% from 30% and set a 15% rate when developers send users elsewhere to complete a purchase.

OpenAI (NASDAQ:OAI) is planning to purchase artificial intelligence chips developed by Alphabet's Google (NASDAQ:GOOG), according to a report published Tuesday by The Information, citing a person familiar with the matter. The potential agreement would expand the commercial relationship between the two companies as demand for AI computing infrastructure continues to increase. The reported plans come as major technology companies commit substantial capital to data centres, processors and other infrastructure required to develop and operate advanced artificial intelligence models. Financial terms and other details of the proposed purchases were not disclosed. Google did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours, while OpenAI declined to comment. The potential chip purchases would represent another development in the relationship between OpenAI and Google, which compete in artificial intelligence products and internet search. Despite that competition, the companies have increasingly established commercial arrangements involving computing infrastructure and AI services. Last week, OpenAI announced that it would make its frontier artificial intelligence models available through Google Cloud. The agreement provides another distribution channel for OpenAI's advanced models while expanding the range of AI services available through Google's cloud platform. The reported plan to purchase Google-designed chips would extend the relationship into semiconductor procurement. Google (GOOG, GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), and Amazon (AMZN) have one big, collective task on their digital shoulders this week as they report their quarterly earnings: They need to justify the AI spending boom. The stakes are high — these companies lead a week of corporate results that account for more than a third of the S&P 500's (^GSPC) earnings Like Meta (META) before them, the biggest question they'll face is likely about AI spending. Specifically, what that number is and how it compares to the expected returns. "All eyes will be on AI monetization vs. spending, with hyperscalers' 2027 capex estimates already revised up by nearly 90% YTD," Bank of America strategist Savita Subramanian wrote in a note on Tuesday. Tech execs having to justify their huge AI spending has been a feature of earnings reports for the past two years. Skeptical investors are eager to see returns on investment, and Wall Street has been rattled by cycles of doubt. But conditions in the economy and the investing environments have changed, heightening the urgency to show results. The recent tech sell-off has thrown AI financing into the spotlight. Companies leading the data center build-out have flagged. And investors have expressed mixed feelings about tech giants like Meta selling shares and borrowing to finance their AI ambitions. The massive demand for financing has increased the competition for capital. That has put pressure on tech companies to preemptively raise enormous sums of money, especially as Wall Street prepares to shepherd the blockbuster IPOs of two frontier AI labs — Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) as soon as next month and OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) likely next year. AI business dynamics are also changing. The era of tokenmaxxing is officially over. Businesses are becoming pickier and choosier with their AI spending — scaling back, using less expensive models, and experimenting with different services. The slowdown in token spending among corporations suggests the lavish appetite for compute only existed when it was effectively free. And so, if the demand for compute isn't infinite and is actually price-sensitive, that means justifying AI costs will be more important. Lastly, Meta's Muse and the early success of personal assistant AI agents have scrambled product priorities. Meta has reoriented the entire company around the division behind Muse and envisions its operations becoming a massive service network and revenue engine. The cash might not come now or even soon, but it will flow, the bull thesis goes. Zuckerberg might have a mixed record, but his company is behind him. And he had the benefit of moving first. The other tech giants this week will have to come up with answers too. Follow Hamza Shaban on X @hshaban.

Alphabet's (GOOGL) Google and Apple (AAPL) were fined 42.9 billion won ($32 million) and 20.81 billion won, respectively, by the Korea Media and Communications Commission for practices prohibited under the Telecommunications Business Act, including forcing app developers to use specific in-app payment systems, the regulator said Wednesday. Inspections and investigations launched in 2022 found app market operators conducted prohibited practices, including forcing specific payment methods, unfairly delaying app reviews and, in Apple's case, impairing users' interests, the regulator said. Both companies charged a 26% commission for the use of third-party payment methods while limiting access to features available through their own payment services, effectively forcing developers to use only their own in-app payments, the regulator said. Apple was also found to have imposed discriminatory commissions on domestic and overseas app developers between July 2015 and January 2023, the commission said. The commission said it also issued corrective orders requiring both companies to revise the terms and conditions of their contracts with app developers. Google and Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment from MT Newswires.

South Korea fines Google and Apple over unfair app market practices

No summary available

SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — South Korea on Wednesday fined Alphabet's Google and Apple a combined 63.7 billion won ($47.6 million), saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews. The Korea Media ...

SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — South Korea on Wednesday fined Alphabet's Google and Apple a combined 63.7 billion won ($47.6 million), saying they abused their dominance in app store markets by forcing local developers onto their own payment systems and by unfairly delaying app reviews. The Korea Media and Communications Commission, the country's media and telecommunications regulator, spent years investigating the U.S. tech giants for allegedly violating a 2021 law that prohibits app store operators from forcing developers to use specific payment systems. The commission fined Google 42.9 billion won ($32 million) and Apple 20.8 billion won ($15.5 million) and ordered both companies to let South Korean developers use external payment links within their apps and to improve their app review procedures. In a statement to The Associated Press, Apple said it "respectfully" disagrees with the decision, arguing that its current practices comply with South Korean law and that it is evaluating its legal options. Apple said its in-app payment system allows users to make secure transactions while protecting them from predatory tactics and fraud and that such safeguards that could potentially be lost when paying through alternative methods. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The commission said Google and Apple unfairly pushed app developers toward their own in-app payment systems while barring payments through external websites. Although the companies technically allowed third-party payment systems within apps, they charged developers a 26% commission and withheld some features available through their own systems, effectively forcing developers to use only their in-app payment systems, the commission said. The commission said it also found instances where the companies delayed app reviews without clearly explaining to developers the reasons for the delays or when reviews would resume. It also accused Apple of charging South Korean developers higher commissions than developers elsewhere from 2015 to January 2023. South Korea has for years closely scrutinized the business practices of foreign technology companies operating in its market. In 2021, it became the first country to enforce a law prohibiting app market operators such as Google and Apple from requiring users to use their own in-app payment systems.

It's a breathtaking abuse of leverage that is potentially anti-competitive. The new terms were first reported by Nieman Lab on Oct. 15, triggering an outcry from news publishers around the world, including in Canada. Under the terms originally scheduled to go into effect on Oct. 30, Meta would be able to use web scrapers to collect content from accounts that manage pages and groups, run advertisements, push marketing messages and use the platform's business account dashboard. There's no opt-out. Meta's message to businesses is blunt: "If you do not agree to the updated terms, please stop all access or use of our products for business or commercial purposes." According to the Nieman Lab report, Meta's original plan appeared to leave the door open to use the scraped material to train its AI systems. Following the backlash, the company delayed implementation till Nov. 20 and revised the language, removing the word "train" and limiting the stated purpose to "advertising and business products." Meta said the delay will give it more time to explain the changes, but legal experts have noted that the new wording doesn't specifically rule out AI training. For news publishers, the threat is stark — their journalism could be used to improve AI products that may ultimately compete with them for readers, advertising and revenue. They would be helping build the very tools that undermine their businesses. But the problem extends well beyond the news industry. At its core, this is a reminder of what happens when a dominant platform can dictate terms to users that have few realistic alternatives. Publishers have had fraught relations with Meta for years, particularly in Canada. In 2023, they lobbied for the Online News Act, which sought to make certain digital platforms compensate news organizations for making their content available. Meta responded by blocking news content on Facebook and Instagram in Canada. Nevertheless, news organizations continue to maintain business accounts for advertising, marketing, communications and other commercial purposes, which leaves them in an awkward position. They may no longer be able to share news links as they once did, but they still have reasons to use Meta's services. Abandoning its apps altogether means sacrificing access to customers, audiences and business tools.

Tesla's (NASDAQ: TSLA) third-quarter earnings report came with at least one notable surprise -- the company announced that it generated $1.53 billion in free cash flow, just one quarter after burning through more than $1 billion in cash. That's certainly encouraging news for a company spending heavily on artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous vehicles, and humanoid robots. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » But before investors get too excited, there's something important buried in those numbers. Tesla's free cash flow fell 62% from a year earlier, and the positive result was largely due to lower capital expenditure (capex) than forecast. That raises some interesting questions about how Tesla intends to finance Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk's ambitious plans -- and what those investments could mean for Tesla stock. In the third quarter, Tesla generated $6.26 billion in operating cash flow, essentially matching the $6.24 billion it produced a year earlier. That was an improvement from the $4.7 billion generated in the second quarter. But capital expenditures tell a different story. Tesla's capex totaled $4.73 billion during the quarter, down from $5.79 billion in the second quarter. That helped turn a $1.09 billion free cash flow deficit into a $1.53 billion surplus. The result was also considerably better than Wall Street expected. According to Tesla's own pre-earnings average estimate, analysts had anticipated about $7.77 billion in third-quarter capex and negative free cash flow of $4.51 billion. Instead, Tesla spent roughly $3 billion less than expected. That's a big difference. And while generating positive free cash flow is preferable to burning cash, spending less money doesn't necessarily mean the underlying business has become more profitable. In fact, Tesla's third-quarter operating income fell 56% year over year to $718 million, while net income attributable to common shareholders declined 43% to $787 million. The company is generating cash, but its earnings remain under pressure. Earlier this year, Tesla announced it would make more than $25 billion in capex. But during the third-quarter earnings call, Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja lowered that outlook to about $20 billion.

Peter Goodricke thought he'd found a great deal. In August and September of 2024, the New Zealand electrical engineer bought two damaged Tesla Model 3s through a vehicle auction. The insurers of the cars had written them off and deregistered them, believing them to be beyond repair — or at least not worth the expense of doing so. Goodricke repaired the cars, though, and both passed the inspection required for re-registration. But because the cars had been structurally damaged at one point, the company sent an over-the-air update that disabled fast-charging. The only way to recharge them was with a regular power point, a process that can take days. Goodricke instead decided to take the company to court, alleging it had breached the country's fair trading act. The claim was dismissed. And when he appealed that to the country's high court, he was not only denied again, but ordered to pay Tesla around $27,000 NZD in court costs (approximately $15,000). "Tesla, unlike most car manufacturers, retains the ability to reach into individual vehicles long after their sale and make alterations which limit their functionality," the judge wrote. "That power is remarkable and may be exercised only in the most tightly constrained circumstances." Tesla did not respond to a Moneywise request for comment on the case. While it was a disappointing conclusion for Goodricke, Tesla has never made a secret of its policies — and that worked in its favor in this case. The company's Unsupported Vehicle Policy is available on its Website and clearly reads, "Vehicles with clean titles may still be classified as unsupported. Until Tesla can confirm that the vehicle complies with Tesla's safety standards and vehicle specifications, Tesla does not perform or support repairs involving the high voltage battery systems in the vehicle." The concern, the company says, is safety related. Vehicles that Tesla has not confirmed comply with its safety standards could damage a Supercharger or might not be safe to drive, the company says.

Tesla's (NASDAQ: TSLA) capital expenditures (capex) totaled $4.73 billion in Q3, more than double the $2.25 billion it spent a year earlier. That's a substantial increase, although considerably less than the roughly $7.5 billion Wall Street anticipated. Tesla also reduced its full-year capital spending forecast from more than $25 billion to about $20 billion. But that's still more than twice the $8.53 billion it spent in 2025. So where is all that money going? Let's take a closer look. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Tesla has been rapidly expanding its artificial intelligence (AI) computing infrastructure at Gigafactory outside of Austin, Texas. This is what's training the neural networks powering full self-driving, Cybercab autonomous vehicles, and Optimus humanoid robots. And it requires thousands of specialized processors, servers, networking equipment, cooling systems, and electrical infrastructure. Tesla is also investing in Cybercab manufacturing and its robotaxi fleet. Unlike vehicles sold directly to consumers, Tesla robotaxis require up-front investment in vehicles, charging infrastructure, and maintenance infrastructure before generating transportation revenue. The potential payoff is significant. Estimates from S&P Global Market Intelligence and Visible Alpha suggest Tesla's robotaxi business could generate about $42.4 billion in annual revenue by 2030. At a hypothetical 20% operating margin, that would produce roughly $8.5 billion in annual operating profit. Tesla could also generate recurring revenue from its full self-driving software. At $99 per month, 5 million paying subscribers would generate about $5.9 billion annually. Of course, these projections depend on regulatory approvals, technological improvements, and customers adopting the services in substantial numbers. While I'm optimistic on all three fronts, there are no guarantees. Tesla is also investing in manufacturing capacity for Optimus, its humanoid robot designed to perform physical tasks in factories and other workplaces. In Q3, Tesla began production of Optimus at its Fremont, California, facility, where it's converting manufacturing space previously used for the Model S and Model X vehicles. The company has discussed eventually producing as many as 1 million robots annually at Fremont. But getting there will require significant investment in production lines, motors, sensors, batteries, and specialized manufacturing equipment. And that stuff isn't cheap.

If you can't beat tech companies, join them. General Motors (GM) said Tuesday it will move its stock listing from the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq, home of many of Silicon Valley's biggest names, in an effort to repitch the legacy Detroit automaker as a tech-forward enterprise. Even sitting close to names like Apple (AAPL) and Amazon (AMZN) can have a spillover effect, as investors cling to the excitement around AI and tech's overall influence in steering the market. Labels matter — remember Domino's (DPZ) identity as "a technology company that happens to sell pizza?" Walmart (WMT), another name you might not associate with cutting-edge tech, made the same change to the Nasdaq earlier this year as it embraces its own AI and advertising transformation. "GM's customer-focused, technology-driven strategy is creating value for our stockholders, making Nasdaq a natural home for our listing as we grow," said Paul Jacobson, the company's CFO, in a statement on Tuesday. The undisputed heavyweight champion of this move is Elon Musk. Tesla (TSLA) hasn't been a "car company" for years — certainly if you look at its valuation — and SpaceX (SPCX) is no longer a rocket company. (Still, GM has done well.) And investors have bought these arguments. Both companies have valuations commensurate with being an AI/robotics/robotaxi giant or an AI/datacenter/chipmaker giant. A much-talked-about merger with SpaceX would put an even finer point on what Tesla is. Of course, GM does not have these activities to make its case. But in some respects the shift makes sense. Newer vehicles have enhanced safety and steering features that make driving meaningfully different than sitting behind the wheel of the car you got your license in. GM, like other automakers, is outfitting its vehicles with more sophisticated software and sensors. The company announced last week it's working to reduce its development cycle by half through AI tools and virtualization. Some observers are skeptical of the new sales pitch, however. "Cars are the first robots out there in the wild," Envorso founder Adrian Balfour said on Yahoo Finance's Morning Hang on Tuesday. "If it was a data play or if it was a robotics play, I could really see it. But without that, I'm not sure." Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Goldberg's priority is completing a merger rather than holding out for a particular price. "Again, it doesn't make any difference to me. I just want to get it done," he said. Goldberg said investors should consider the value of the shares they would receive alongside the price assigned to their Tesla holdings. "The lower the premium, the higher the value of the SpaceX stock that you get in exchange," he said. "So you guys are so focused on the price of your Tesla shares. He sees SpaceX's opportunity as nearer-term, while Tesla's longer-term potential carries greater uncertainty. "And therefore, even though Tesla may be worth more over time than SpaceX, the SpaceX opportunity is right today. So why not combine the value today with the value tomorrow?" he said. Goldberg also said that combining the companies' assets and cash flows could help finance a computing buildout he estimated could require between $500 billion and $1 trillion, depending on its scale. Goldberg said his position had attracted bitter pushback from Tesla investors focused on their shares' current value and expectations of much higher future prices. "I mean, it's in everybody's interest to merge these companies, you know, and give equal value. However, they can't see it, and they're going to vote against it as a result," he said.

For years, investors wondered what would happen to Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRKA) (NYSE: BRKB) when longtime CEO Warren Buffett stepped down. It was assumed that a Buffett premium was being applied to the stock, given the CEO's impressive track record as an investor. At first, that was true, with the stock falling on the news of his pending departure at the end of 2025. But as 2026 draws to a close, the market's view appears to be changing. And even with the stock now near an all-time high, it could still be worth buying. Here's why. The big worry was that Buffett was the key to Berkshire Hathaway's success. Obviously, Buffett's investment approach helped to build the company, but it is a very different business now than it was when Buffett first took over as CEO. Today, Berkshire Hathaway is a massively diversified conglomerate, with businesses in insurance, utilities, energy, transportation, housing, retail, and manufacturing, among others. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » At a time when investors are worried about the market, Berkshire Hathaway's diversification and focus on fairly simple-to-understand cash-generating businesses provide something of a safe haven. In fact, investors are increasingly worried about the high-tech companies that have driven the market higher, as many are increasingly leaning on their balance sheets to fund growth. To be fair, Berkshire Hathaway has some exposure to technology companies in its stock portfolio, but its operating businesses tend to be much more down-to-earth. And, just as important, new CEO Greg Abel hasn't done anything to compromise the basic nature of Berkshire Hathaway. That said, the balance sheet is another big safety point. At the end of the second quarter, Berkshire Hathaway had more than $350 billion in cash and short-term investments on its balance sheet. That will provide the company with a material cushion in a bear market. And it will also give Abel the firepower to step in and buy while others are fearful during that bear market. That's something Warren Buffett was famous for, and he likely taught his successor the value of both patience and contrarian thinking. There has been a huge change at Berkshire Hathaway with Buffett stepping aside. But roughly 10 months into Greg Abel's tenure, investors are clearly getting more comfortable with the change. And with Wall Street increasingly worried about the tech sector, Berkshire Hathaway's more mundane business profile and huge cash hoard make it look like an attractive alternative for those seeking out a safe-haven investment. Indeed, even with the stock near its all-time highs, it may be worth buying for those who think long term, like Abel and, before him, Buffett.

Typically, more than half of the companies held in Berkshire Hathaway's investment portfolio paid a dividend. Perhaps most importantly, dividend stocks have a lengthy track record of outperforming. The White House puts the housing gap -- the difference between the supply of and demand for available homes -- at 10 million houses. I think Berkshire CEO Greg Abel sees that housing gap as a massive opportunity. So he's investing in homebuilders now when they're cheap. Warren Buffett spent nearly 50 years drinking Pepsi. His son even nicknamed him "Pepsi Warren." Then a neighbor handed him samples of a new cherry-flavored Coca-Cola, and the legendary investor switched sides. The soda switch made for a good story. The stock purchase that followed made history. Buffett began buying Coca-Cola shares in 1988, and Berkshire Hathaway eventually built a 400 million-share position for about $1.3 billion. Today, that stake is worth roughly $37 billion at a share price of $93, while the annual dividend income has climbed to about $848 million. Read more: Warren Buffett explained how he'd turn $10,000 into $30 billion if he were starting over For an investor famous for buying businesses he understands, Coca-Cola was a particularly fitting bet. Buffett knew the product long before he owned a piece of the company. What followed was one of Berkshire Hathaway's most enduring investments. Berkshire Hathaway chairman emeritus Buffett, 96, took control of the company in 1965 and served as chairman for 56 years. He handed the post to his son, Howard Buffett, in September. Greg Abel became CEO in January, and Buffett remains on Berkshire's board of directors. Coca-Cola's troubles started in 1985, when the company replaced its original formula with New Coke. Consumer outrage followed, with thousands of angry calls a day and public protests, until the original recipe returned that year as Coca-Cola Classic. Then came the October 1987 stock market crash, along with a pricing fight with PepsiCo that weighed on the shares. By 1988, Coca-Cola stock had been hit hard. Buffett started buying anyway. Wall Street largely wrote the move off as too expensive and badly timed. Analysts pointed to a price-to-earnings multiple in the mid-teens, which was not the deep-value territory Buffett was known for, and noted that earnings had softened in 1987. More Warren Buffett: Warren Buffett reveals he broke his own investing pattern Warren Buffett has a blunt take on today's market Warren Buffett pulls no punches on stock market for 2026 Buffett saw a different company. He viewed the business, led by CEO Roberto Goizueta and president Don Keough, as a global brand with high returns on capital and enormous room to grow overseas. Berkshire even got permission from the Securities and Exchange Commission to delay disclosing the purchases for a year so the market would not bid the shares up right away. Buffett made his intentions clear to shareholders. "When we own portions of outstanding businesses with outstanding managements, our favorite holding period is forever," Buffett wrote in Berkshire's shareholder letter in 1988.

Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRKA)(NYSE:BRKB) stock is finally back at a record. On Oct. 20, the Class B shares ended at $539.82, inching past a record close from May 2, 2025 -- the day before Warren Buffett told shareholders he planned to hand the CEO job to Greg Abel. As I write, the shares trade near $548, up about 9% this year. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » The new high comes in a year when Berkshire has gone back to buying its own stock. It repurchased nothing in 2025. In the first half of 2026, its buybacks came to around $4.8 billion. And it only buys if its CEO thinks the shares cost less than the business is worth. But Berkshire paid around $476 to $488 a Class B share in May and June. With the stock at least 12% higher today, is it still a buy? Image source: Getty Images. The buying started small. In March, Berkshire repurchased around $234 million of stock at an average of about $487 a Class B share, according to its first-quarter 10-Q. Then it sped up. After a quiet April, Berkshire spent around $740 million on shares in May at an average Class B price of about $476, and about $3.8 billion in June at about $488, for a second-quarter total of about $4.5 billion. And the cover of the second-quarter 10-Q suggests the buying kept going. Berkshire had around 4,550 fewer Class A-equivalent shares outstanding on July 29 than on June 30 (one Class A share equals 1,500 Class B shares). At the $488 to $512 range where the Class B shares closed in July, these repurchased shares total about $3.4 billion of stock in under a month. "We will buy back Berkshire shares when they trade below our estimate of intrinsic value, conservatively determined," Abel said in his first annual letter to shareholders in February. Intrinsic value is Berkshire's term for what the whole business is worth, whatever the stock does day to day. Put another way, every month of buying was Abel saying the shares were cheap at around $476 to $488. I'd argue these purchases tell Berkshire shareholders more about the stock's value than anything else from the company's filings this year. At around $548, the Class B shares cost about 12% more than Berkshire's average price in June and about 15% more than its average in May.

The global energy market has been upended by the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East, sending oil prices sharply higher. Occidental Petroleum (NYSE: OXY) appears better positioned to benefit from high oil prices than Chevron (NYSE: CVX). But don't pull the trigger just yet. There's a very important reason you may want to own Chevron instead, and it may help explain why Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRKA)(NYSE: BRKB) owns both. Warren Buffett once described investing as a baseball game where nobody is calling balls and strikes. The point of that folksy example is to highlight that investors don't have to swing at every pitch; they can just wait for the pitches they like. And that's exactly how Buffett handled Berkshire Hathaway's portfolio, cherry-picking the stocks he wanted inside of it. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » It isn't an accident that Buffett bought Occidental Petroleum and Chevron. It was a conscious decision. And it is important to understand that they are not interchangeable energy investments. There is a notable difference between their business models. Occidental, which most investors just call Oxy, has been focused on growing its production profile. Buffett helped that process along when he assisted Oxy in buying Anadarko Petroleum. In fact, Oxy beat out Chevron for that deal. More recently, Berkshire Hathaway bought Oxy's chemicals business. Berkshire and Oxy have a long history, but the second deal highlights a clear focus on energy production. That's good right now with oil prices at lofty levels. For investors looking to capitalize on high energy prices, Oxy could be a better choice than Chevron. For now. The problem with that story is that oil prices have a long history of being volatile. They rise and fall in often dramatic fashion, driven by factors such as supply and demand, natural and man-made disasters, and geopolitical conflicts. When the event that's driving oil prices higher eventually passes, prices usually fall. When that eventually happens again, as it has every time before, Occidental will be more exposed to the downturn than Chevron. Chevron is one of the world's largest energy companies. It is what is known as an integrated company because it intentionally has exposure across the entire energy value chain, from the upstream (production) through the midstream (pipelines) and all the way to the downstream (chemicals and refining). That diversification helps to soften the impact of oil price swings.

Warren Buffett piled into Apple because he appreciated the brand's loyal customer base and favored the company's market-leading share buyback program. But Apple is in the midst of a multi-year transformation that emphasizes higher-margin subscription services and AI. Prior to his own recent retirement as CEO, Tim Cook shifted Apple's focus to services designed to enhance existing customer loyalty and bolster margins. Double-digit sales growth in the company's services segment should lessen the revenue peaks and valleys commonly seen with major iPhone upgrade cycles. There's also Apple Intelligence, which is the company's generative AI built directly into its operating systems. Embracing these tools should make its physical devices (iPhone, Mac, and iPad) considerably more attractive. Perhaps the biggest change in the wake of Buffett's retirement has been Abel's aggressive purchases of Google parent Alphabet. Though Buffett initiated this position before his retirement, Abel more than tripled it in the first quarter and purchased around $17 billion in additional stock in the second quarter. Alphabet possesses the sustainable moat that Berkshire's current and former bosses often seek out. In September, Google accounted for 90% of global internet search traffic. Maintaining a virtual monopoly in internet search affords the company exceptional ad-pricing power.

"However, large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated ass...

America's biggest bank says the US economy remains strong. Yet JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon has identified five risks that could shake stock and bond markets, even as Wall Street prepares for another Federal Reserve interest-rate decision. "However, large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated asset prices, rising interest rates and geopolitical conditions continue to shift under the surface," Dimon warned in JPMorgan's third-quarter earnings. Here is why each warning matters for investors. US consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier. Gasoline prices jumped 34.2%, squeezing household budgets and raising business costs. Persistent inflation also reduces the purchasing power of fixed bond payments. It gives the Federal Reserve another reason to keep interest rates high. The US recorded a $1.99 trillion budget deficit in fiscal 2026. Washington must borrow heavily to cover the shortfall. More government bonds entering the market can push yields higher, reducing the value of existing bonds and raising borrowing costs across the economy. The AI boom is showing cracks. China's technology-heavy STAR 50 index has lost roughly 40% in under four months. America's Nasdaq fell nearly 6% from its October peak through Friday. Investors are increasingly questioning whether enormous AI investments will deliver enough profit to justify elevated stock valuations. The Fed raised rates in September to 3.75%–4%. Markets expect a pause on October 28, followed by another increase in December. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, pressure corporate profits and typically weigh on existing bond prices. The Middle East conflict has pushed oil prices above $100 a barrel, adding fresh pressure to global inflation. Another energy shock could force the Fed to maintain restrictive rates even as economic growth weakens. For now, JPMorgan's own figures suggest resilience. The bank recorded $2.7 billion in provisions for credit losses, down from $3.4 billion a year earlier. But Dimon's warning raises a troubling question: how long can that resilience survive if all five risks intensify together?
