Intel Corporation INTC is scheduled to report third-quarter 2026 earnings after the closing bell on Oct. 29. In the to-be-reported quarter, the company is likely to have recorded higher revenues from the Datacenter and AI Group (DCAI) segment, owing to the expansion of its AI infrastructure portfolio with three new platforms designed to support agentic AI across data centers, enterprise systems and intelligent edge devices. The DCAI segment seeks to develop leading data center products, including Intel Xeon servers and field-programmable gate array products, while overseeing the overall AI strategy. During the quarter, Intel introduced Diamond Rapids, Crescent Island and Wildcat Lake to address growing AI demands across data centers and intelligent devices. Intel's next-generation Diamond Rapids Xeon processor is designed to support enterprise-scale agentic AI workloads. The Crescent Island is a low-power AI inference GPU based on the Xe3P architecture, featuring 32 Xe cores, 256 XMX engines and up to 480GB of LPDDR5X memory in a 350-watt air-cooled PCIe design. At the edge, the company launched Wildcat Lake as Intel Core Series 3 processors, bringing AI capabilities to laptops and edge devices with two performance cores, four efficiency cores, Xe3 graphics with XMX acceleration and an NPU offering up to 17 TOPS, along with support for LPDDR5X-7467, Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0. These offerings highlight Intel's strategy for addressing AI requirements across infrastructure and devices for a more competitive AI hardware ecosystem. As demand for AI inference grows, Intel is combining optimized hardware and software to deliver scalable, efficient and cost-effective solutions for increasingly complex AI workloads. The company improved its AI inference capabilities with the latest MLPerf Inference v6.1 results, showing performance gains across Intel Xeon 6 processors and Intel Arc Pro B-series GPUs. The results highlight the company's continued efforts to optimize AI frameworks, kernels and serving software for more efficient inference. Intel Xeon 6980P processors delivered 2.4x higher Llama 3.1 8B Server throughput and 56% higher Offline throughput than MLPerf v6.0 using the same hardware setup, reflecting the benefits of software optimization. The increased adoption of Intel processors and NPUs follows the positive feedback of Xeon 6 processors with Performance-cores (P-Cores). This system-on-chip (SoC) has been designed to meet the huge demand for high AI workloads across various sectors. With industry-leading performance across data center workloads and up to two times higher performance in AI processing, the Xeon 6 family delivers the industry's best central processing unit (CPU) for AI at a lower total cost of ownership (TCO). Intel Xeon platforms have reportedly set the benchmark in 5G cloud-native core with substantial performance and power-efficiency improvements, additional power-saving capabilities and easy-to-deploy software. This has driven healthy demand trends from major telecom equipment manufacturers and independent software vendors to optimize and unleash proven power savings for a more sustainable future. These are likely to have generated incremental revenues in the quarter. However, China's purported move to replace U.S.-made chips with domestic alternatives is expected to affect the segment's revenues as Intel derives a significant portion of its revenues from the Asian country. The recent directive to phase out foreign chips from key telecom networks by 2027 underscores Beijing's accelerating efforts to reduce reliance on Western technology amid escalating U.S.-China tensions and tariff wars. As Washington tightens restrictions on high-tech exports to China, Beijing has intensified its push for self-sufficiency in critical industries. This shift poses a dual challenge for Intel, as it faces potential market restrictions and increased competition from domestic chipmakers. In addition, Intel is witnessing intensifying competition in the server, storage and networking markets from its rivals.

Charm™ AI is the enterprise-scale language model trained and served entirely on CPU servers, validated on Intel Xeon 6 processors. SAN DIEGO, Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Symbolic Mind, Inc., an enterprise AI platform company, today announced plans to bring Charm AI to enterprises that need to train and run models inside their own infrastructure. Working with Intel, Symbolic Mind, Inc. has completed a proof-of-concept on Intel Xeon 6 processors and are now taking the result to market. Symbolic Mind's Deep Control™ AI architecture delivers order-of-magnitude reductions in training and inference cost by running both processes on CPU-based servers. Symbolic Mind was able to leverage Intel VTune Profiler and IntelAdvisor in achieving these cost & performance gains. Alongside those, Charm AI learns continuously — accuracy improves as new customer data is added, rather than degrading — and keeps data, models and intellectual property inside the customer's own environment.1 "We are going to deliver our Charm AI model through multiple channels, including but not limited to hyperscaler marketplaces, on-premises deployments and standalone AI server appliances, powered by Intel Xeon processors, especially for regulated industries such as finance, insurance and healthcare," said Vamsi Sistla, Symbolic Mind CEO and Co-Founder. "Enterprises are looking for practical ways to leverage the power of AI without having to overcomplicate their IT infrastructure deployments," said Lynn Comp, Intel, Head of Xeon Market Readiness. "Symbolic Mind's efforts underscores how organizations can train and run AI entirely on Intel Xeon 6 processors, enabling AI adoption on existing CPU-based infrastructure while maintaining control of their data, costs and operations." Symbolic Mind plans to offer an AI-Ready Rack as a turnkey solution for corporate customers to train and run their own models. A small number of racks of CPU servers provides enough computational power to train and run enterprise AI models. 1 Technical detail and proof points for Charm AI on Intel® Xeon® 6 processors: Symbolic Mind — Charm Frontier AI on CPUs, Partner Brief (intel.com) ABOUT SYMBOLIC MIND, INC. Symbolic Mind, Inc. is enterprise software that lets companies build and own their own frontier AI. Its patent-pending Deep Control™ neuro-symbolic architecture trains and serves purpose-built, domain-specific models on commodity CPU servers, so customers can train on their own data inside their own private cloud and own, audit and control the models that result. Symbolic Mind's Charm™ AI model uses linear computational complexity rather than the quadratic attention complexity of transformer models. Founded in 2023 and incorporated in Delaware, the company has offices in the United States (Seattle, Washington), Israel, India and Brazil. Learn more at symbolicmind.ai.

Did The Market Read Intel Right?

The company's latest report during that period arrived on July 23 for fiscal Q2 2026. Two areas of Intel's busines...

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Intel (INTC) stock returned 136.3% in the year to October 26, 2026, compared with 14.3% for the S&P 500. The company's latest report during that period arrived on July 23 for fiscal Q2 2026. Two areas of Intel's business warrant a close look: its data center chips and its chip-making unit, Intel Foundry. So has Intel's business changed as much as its share price? Intel's Data Center Sales Are Growing Fast Part of the business has changed, beginning with data center chips. Management said on the July 23 call that Intel's data center sales reached $6.3 billion in fiscal Q2 2026, up 59% from a year earlier. That marks a different pace from fiscal 2025, when the same business grew 4.9% for the full year. The shift also extends to the whole company's profit from operations. Intel posted a 12.2% operating margin in fiscal Q2 2026, compared with an operating loss equal to 10.0% of revenue in fiscal Q2 2025. Management said on the call that this was the seventh quarter in a row that Intel beat its own financial expectations. Intel Foundry Is Still Losing Money The loss is shrinking, but it is still large. Management said Intel Foundry lost $2.1 billion at the operating level in fiscal Q2 2026, which was $348 million less than in the preceding quarter. Management also said factory output on Intel 18A, the process behind the company's Core Ultra Series 3 processors, ran about 25% above target. Outside customers still represent a small portion of the unit's sales. They paid $293 million of Intel Foundry's $5.8 billion in revenue that quarter, meaning the foundry still produces mostly for Intel itself. On the same call, management raised its 2026 capital spending outlook to more than $20 billion, citing strong customer demand signals. So the spending is rising before outside customers have become a large part of the foundry's sales. How Much Are Investors Paying For Intel Now? Investors now pay 8.1 times Intel's sales, compared with 3.2 times for the S&P 500. Intel traded at 1.8 times sales at the end of June 2025, when the stock closed at $22.40, before the rally began that summer.. Some of the rally has already reversed: Intel stock fell 26.4% from September 25 to October 26, 2026, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.8%. That multiple represents a price for revenue, not for profit. If data center growth slows or the foundry loss stops shrinking, investors are left paying well above the market's multiple for sales that do not yet produce a net profit.

Oracle, IBM and Intel Have Opted Out of OKX-ICE Stock Tokens, Venue’s Own Notice Shows

No summary available

The tokenized stock venue run by Intercontinental Exchange and OKX now counts 26 companies that have objected to tokenized versions of their shares trading on it, according to a revised public notice the venue published dated Oct. 26. That is four more than the 22 objectors Unchained reported on Oct...

The tokenized stock venue run by Intercontinental Exchange and OKX now counts 26 companies that have objected to tokenized versions of their shares trading on it, according to a revised public notice the venue published dated Oct. 26. That is four more than the 22 objectors Unchained reported on Oct. 23. The last four names on the notice's list are IBM, IonQ, Oracle and Intel. Moderna, Cisco and Marvell Technology also appear. None of those seven were named in Unchained's earlier coverage. The full list also includes Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs, Broadcom, Verizon, Wells Fargo, Arm Holdings and Intuit. The notice gives no reason for any objection and no launch date. Get Unchained's crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter. The SEC's tokenized securities venue exemption, an order dated Sept. 17 that is set to expire Sept. 17, 2031, lets an issuer keep its stock off such a venue. When a third party unaffiliated with the company makes the token, the venue must notify the issuer and wait at least 30 calendar days before trading starts. If an issuer objects in writing during that window, the token can't trade. The venue gets five business days after that to list the objection in an updated notice. The venue is operated by OKXICE LLC, a Texas company owned 50% by ICE and 50% by OKC USA Holding, the joint venture the two firms formed. Trading will run through permissioned Uniswap v4 pools on XLayer, which will be open only to wallets holding a soulbound token (SBT) that OKXICE issues. The notice states the venue is not registered with the SEC for these activities and "is not subject to Regulation NMS." The notice repeats risk warnings that have appeared in earlier versions. Decrypt reported on Oct. 25, citing the Oct. 23 notice, that administrators could change the venue's contracts with no warning to users and that the contract controlling trading access had been reviewed only in-house. "The SBT smart contract has been audited internally, but not by external auditors," the notice says in its risk section. A second contract, the hook that checks those tokens on every trade, is to be audited internally and by Certified Kernel Tech LLC before it goes live. Administrator keys for the contracts are managed by OKX Technology Inc., and contract changes "take effect without a timelock, so TSV Participants may receive no advance notice of an upgrade," according to the notice. On investor protection, the venue writes that whether tokens "held in a self-custodied wallet would be treated as customer property or protected by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation is uncertain, and any recovery could be delayed or incomplete."

Under the SEC's exemption for tokenized stock venues, an order dated Sept. 17, a venue has to notify an issuer before it trades a token of that company's stock created by an unaffiliated third party. The tally has risen with each revision: nine on Oct. 15, when five, including Broadcom and Verizon, opted out, then 16 on Oct. 19 and 22 on Oct. 23, when six, including Wells Fargo, Arm and Intuit, were added. By investing in Meta, Nvidia and AMD secure a massive customer for their high-margin AI accelerators. Meta, in turn, secures prioritized access to essential compute power to scale its rapidly growing Muse AI agent, which runs on Nvidia infrastructure and AMD's EPYC processors. This creates a feedback loop: Meta's AI success drives demand for chips, which funds further chip innovation, benefiting the entire supply chain within the AI ecosystem. This is, in fact, part of a broader trend in 2026 where tech giants are vertically integrating via capital injection. News Highlights AMD and Meta collaborate across CPUs, GPUs, networking, systems and software to power Meta services and AI infrastructure AMD Helios rackscale solutions will power Meta's leading frontier models and services AMD technology is the compute engine of choice for Muse and AMD technologies provide Day-0 support for leading Meta models SANTA CLARA, Calif., Oct. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) today highlighted its deep strategic partnership with Meta, announcing AMD Helios™ rackscale solutions are running at Meta, AMD EPYC™ processors power Meta's Muse AI agent, and AMD technologies provide Day-0 support for Meta models including Muse Spark Open and Muse Glimmer. This builds on years of co-design and collaboration between the two companies across AMD EPYC™ processors, AMD Instinct™ GPUs, AMD Pensando™ networking and AMD ROCm™ AI infrastructure. "Meta is a strategic partner for AMD, and we have built this partnership through years of deep technical collaboration – from EPYC processors powering Meta's infrastructure to Instinct GPUs and open software supporting its AI workloads," said Lisa Su, Chair and CEO, AMD. "With Helios now running at Meta, we are taking that partnership to a new scale in the superintelligence era. Together, we are building and deploying infrastructure at gigawatt scale and shaping future generations of silicon, software and systems to enable Meta's most ambitious superintelligence models and services." "AMD has been a key partner in building out the compute that's running our frontier models," said Mark Zuckerberg, founder and CEO, Meta, "We're making big investments in the computing power that will enable us to bring personal superintelligence to everyone, and AMD plays an important role in that." AMD Powering Meta Infrastructure, Today AMD technology powers Meta's infrastructure across compute, networking, systems and software. Initial AMD Helios rackscale solutions are installed and being tested by Meta on the path to a broader deployment in the near future. AMD EPYC processors support the dedicated computing environments behind Meta's Muse personal AI agent. Meta has deployed millions of EPYC processors across multiple generations and is a lead customer for 6th Gen EPYC™ CPUs. The companies are also collaborating on future generations, including "Verano." AMD Instinct GPUs are currently used in production in Meta's infrastructure for training, ranking and recommendation engines. Meta was also an early definition customer for the AMD Instinct™ MI450 architecture, and it will deploy a custom AMD Instinct GPU that is optimized for its workloads. The collaboration is also informing future AMD platforms, including AMD Instinct™ MI500 series GPUs and next-generation rack-scale systems. AMD and Meta have worked together to advance ROCm through PyTorch to ensure that developers can leverage AMD GPUs right out of the box. As well, AMD delivered Day-0 support for Meta's Muse Spark Open models on AMD Instinct GPUs and for Muse Glimmer on AMD Ryzen™ AI PCs and AMD Radeon™ GPUs. AMD and Meta have expanded their software collaboration to large-scale AI training, optimizing recommendation models on AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs and contributing improvements to PyTorch, Triton and ROCm for other developers to use.

AMD and Nvidia Split the AI Chip Market. 1 Stock Is Far Cheaper Today.

No summary available

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) are two of the biggest names in the artificial intelligence (AI) chip market. Their graphics processing units (GPUs) are the most popular options, and each is growing rapidly. However, from an investment standpoint, they are fundamentall...

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) and Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) are two of the biggest names in the artificial intelligence (AI) chip market. Their graphics processing units (GPUs) are the most popular options, and each is growing rapidly. However, from an investment standpoint, they are fundamentally different, especially when price tags are considered. Nvidia is far cheaper than AMD, and this is something that investors can't ignore. I think that makes Nvidia the superior buy, but is there more to this picture? Let's take a look. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Nvidia and AMD both make GPUs, which are general purpose computing units that can excel in just about any situation. This makes them the workhorse of the AI computing landscape, even as other custom AI alternatives grow more popular. Those custom chips are only meant to run one type of workload and will never fully replace GPUs. In the early days of the AI arms race, Nvidia's products were far superior, which allowed it to capture an early lead. While AMD has improved its game, Nvidia's early lead has been tough to overcome. However, the law of large numbers suggests that the larger a company gets, the harder it is to grow. Therefore, if AMD is smaller, then it should be able to grow faster than Nvidia. If everything else is equal, a faster-growing stock will lead to better long-term returns, which would push AMD ahead of Nvidia as an investment option. The problem is, it isn't happening. Nvidia is far larger than AMD. Nvidia's data center division (the sector most exposed to AI) saw revenue of $89 billion during the second quarter of its fiscal year (FY) 2027 (ended July 26). AMD's Q2 (which ended on June 30) saw revenue of $6.7 billion. The company's financial calendars are about one month apart, so this isn't a perfect comparison, but it's the best that investors can do. With AMD's data center division being more than 10 times smaller than Nvidia, it should have no problem growing faster, but Nvidia's growth in Q2 was 117% versus AMD's 107%. While both companies are each delivering strong results, Nvidia is clearly growing faster despite its much larger size. But there's more to this analysis. AMD and Nvidia also have non-data-center segments. However, Nvidia's other businesses are far smaller, and data center revenue accounts for the majority of Nvidia's $96.2 billion total. AMD's Q2 revenue was $11.5 billion, so other divisions make up a far higher percentage of its revenue. The problem is that these product lines aren't growing nearly as fast, so AMD's overall growth rate significantly lags Nvidia's.

Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise Estimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. Our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction) -- has this insight at its core. The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier. Thus, a positive or negative Earnings ESP reading theoretically indicates the likely deviation of the actual earnings from the consensus estimate. However, the model's predictive power is significant for positive ESP readings only.

SK Hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY), the South Korean memory chipmaker, reported its third-quarter earnings on Oct. 28, and the results didn't disappoint. But while the company is marking a record-setting quarter and a big jump in stock price today, I think Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) shareholders have plenty of reasons to be excited as well. SK Hynix reported that its production of dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is effectively sold out through 2029, with memory shortages expected to last through 2030. The company said long-term supply agreements, combined with customer contracts still under discussion, account for its expected production over the next three years. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » "We expect it to be difficult to fully meet customers' volume requirements in the near term," Chief Financial Officer Woo-hyun Kim said on the company's earnings call. "Given the complexities involved in implementing leading-edge processes and the lead times required to construct new production facilities, a situation where supply cannot keep up with demand is expected to persist for some time, a constraint projected to continue through 2030." That's outstanding news for SK Hynix. But it could be equally important for Micron, which competes with SK Hynix and Samsung in the global memory market. Image source: Getty Images. Micron Executive Vice President and Chief Business Officer Sumit Sadana told investors at KeyBanc's Technology Leadership Forum in August that calendar 2027 would be "even tighter" than 2026. Sadana also said Micron had no clear indication of when memory supply would finally catch up with demand. Now SK Hynix is telling investors essentially the same thing: The memory shortage issue won't disappear anytime soon. And that could give Micron considerable pricing power. HBM is a specialized form of DRAM that stacks memory chips vertically to deliver the enormous bandwidth required by AI accelerators. Micron manufactures both HBM and conventional DRAM, and there's an interesting relationship between the two products. Producing HBM requires considerably more manufacturing capacity than producing the same amount of conventional DRAM.

Seasoned drug delivery and product development leader formerly at Lilly and AstraZeneca to advance Micron Biomedical's transition from platform technology to commercial product company Anand Subramony, Ph.D. joins Micron Biomedical ATLANTA, Oct. 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Micron Biomedical, a clinical-stage biotech company developing next-generation thermostable vaccines and therapeutics, today announced the appointment of Anand Subramony, Ph.D., as Executive Vice President, Global Product Development and Combination Product Commercialization. Dr. Subramony will report to the Chief Executive Officer and lead product development, regulatory strategy, and commercialization of Micron Biomedical's owned vaccines and therapeutics, as well as its partnership strategy. "As demand for novel biologics that can be manufactured, stored, transported and self-administered without cold-chain and injection-related barriers of traditional injectable medicines expands beyond vaccines to areas including biosecurity measures, GLP-1s, and other combination products, Micron is committed to advancing an expanding pipeline of accessible and life-changing biotech innovations," said Steven Damon, CEO of Micron Biomedical. "Anand brings decades of experience turning innovative drug delivery technologies into successful medicines at Lilly and AstraZeneca, and his leadership, combined with our strong clinical evidence, solidified backing by government and industry partners and commercial-scale manufacturing facility, position Micron Biomedical to bring a new generation of treatments to the market at scale." Dr. Subramony brings 27 years of experience developing drug-device combination products and novel delivery technologies at Eli Lilly and Company, AstraZeneca/MedImmune, Novartis, Dr. Reddy's Laboratories and Johnson & Johnson's ALZA Corporation. Most recently, as Vice President of Delivery, Device and Connection Solutions at Lilly, he built the company's early development organization, Drug Delivery and New Product Innovation, and advanced new delivery technologies and device platforms for incretin medicines, large volume biologics delivery, deep understanding of injection physiology, nanomedicine platforms, and other programs that progressed to later stage development towards commercialization. Earlier, at AstraZeneca and MedImmune, Dr. Subramony established the device development group (2014-2017) and led foundational device work for all the biologics including prefilled syringe, autoinjectors, and advanced an oral peptide (GLP-1) program to the clinic. He also founded the early vision for connected-device and digital health strategy including remote patient monitoring using digital biomarkers, and provided leadership to a peptide based targeted nanoparticle platform. His leadership at Novartis signified the establishment of a global drug delivery organization (NDT) that focused on delivery solutions for portfolio compounds through data driven feasibility studies with external technologies to create differentiated medicine. While at Dr. Reddys, Dr. Subramony established the center of excellence in Materials Science and Drug Delivery and provided leadership to the internal development and launch of a dry powder inhaler, Redihaler, for the generic market. He began his career in transdermal delivery at ALZA, where he was a lead contributor to two launched transdermal systems and worked on several drug delivery solutions across various interfaces.

Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) is introducing quarterly profit-sharing bonuses on top of its annual incentives, Reuters reported October 22. Half will be paid in cash, while the other half comes in company shares that vest after a year. For older workers already collecting Social Security, those stock awards could put part of their benefits at risk. Imagine a 63-year-old at another company who collects Social Security and works part time. His salary falls below the annual earnings limit, and he figures the stock portion of his bonuses doesn't count as income until he sells the shares. That assumption could cost him. Stock awarded for work can count as wages even when he doesn't sell a single share. The timing depends on the award's terms and when he earned it. Stock awarded for work is generally taxable compensation. But when an employer requires someone to stay on the job before the shares become theirs, the tax usually comes later, when those restrictions end. That's why the date an employee receives an award isn't necessarily the date it counts as pay. Selling the shares later is a separate matter. Once their value has been taxed as compensation, that amount generally becomes the starting point for calculating any additional gain or loss when the employee sells them. ------ Free Report, Just Released Why Didn't MU Make The Top 10 List? 24/7 Wall St has helped investors make money for over two decades, and our top analysts just finished ranking the definitive Top 10 Stocks To Buy Now. Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Image source: Getty Images. Nvidia isn't the only company to design GPUs, but it is the market leader. This is for a few reasons. This early start offered it the chance to fine-tune its technology and develop relationships with key customers. Today, Nvidia's commitment to annual innovation keeps it in the No. 1 spot -- as rivals develop a GPU to beat the current Nvidia product, Nvidia has already moved on to its next update. This AI powerhouse, thanks to its CUDA parallel computing platform and vast array of products and services, offers customers everything to suit their AI needs. These customers, already using Nvidia platforms, might find it easier and more cost-effective to stick with this provider, building on systems they already have operating. All of this has made Nvidia an obvious superstar of the AI revolution. TSMC wins when Nvidia wins. Demand for advanced packaging services is extending beyond graphics processing units, according to the report. The newspaper identified server central processing units and custom application-specific integrated circuits as additional sources of demand for CoWoS packaging. These developments are increasing the range of semiconductor products competing for advanced packaging capacity. The report also noted that AI processors require longer testing periods, adding to the workload of semiconductor packaging and testing providers. The combination of additional chip categories and extended testing requirements is contributing to capacity constraints across the industry. Equipment delivery schedules have also lengthened as manufacturers seek to expand advanced packaging production. According to the Commercial Times, equipment lead times have increased to between six and eight months, compared with approximately three to six months previously. The longer delivery periods reflect difficulties in expanding production capacity quickly enough to meet demand.

The recommendations of Wall Street analysts are often relied on by investors when deciding whether to buy, sell, or hold a stock. Media reports about these brokerage-firm-employed (or sell-side) analysts changing their ratings often affect a stock's price. Do they really matter, though? Let's take a look at what these Wall Street heavyweights have to say about TSMC (TSM) before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage. TSMC currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.21, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 19 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.21 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy. Of the 19 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 16 are Strong Buy and two are Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 84.2% and 10.5% of all recommendations. Check price target & stock forecast for TSMC here>>> While the ABR calls for buying TSMC, it may not be wise to make an investment decision solely based on this information. Several studies have shown limited to no success of brokerage recommendations in guiding investors to pick stocks with the best price increase potential. Do you wonder why? As a result of the vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover, their analysts tend to rate it with a strong positive bias. According to our research, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations for every "Strong Sell" recommendation. This means that the interests of these institutions are not always aligned with those of retail investors, giving little insight into the direction of a stock's future price movement. It would therefore be best to use this information to validate your own analysis or a tool that has proven to be highly effective at predicting stock price movements. Zacks Rank, our proprietary stock rating tool with an impressive externally audited track record, categorizes stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), and is an effective indicator of a stock's price performance in the near future. Therefore, using the ABR to validate the Zacks Rank could be an efficient way of making a profitable investment decision. In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures. The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.

Taiwan Semiconductor and ASML Are Incredible, but 1 of These Monopoly Chip Stocks Is Far Safer.

Both are essentially monopolies for different reasons, but each is an incredible business and has rewarded shareholders with strong stock performance. However, ...

There are few companies on the market more impressive than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM) and ASML Holding (NASDAQ: ASML). Both are essentially monopolies for different reasons, but each is an incredible business and has rewarded shareholders with strong stock performance. However, these two aren't the same from an investment standpoint. One is far safer, and it all boils down to how much success is priced into the stock. I think Taiwan Semiconductor is the far safer bet for multiple reasons, making it the better investment right now. Here's why. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » There are different types of monopolies, and not all of them are viewed the same way. When it comes to monopolies, ASML is about as good as it gets. It is the only company in the world with the technology to make extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. These machines are about as big as a school bus and cost hundreds of millions of dollars. EUV machines are used by chip fabricators, such as Taiwan Semiconductor, to lay down tiny electrical traces on chips. These traces are microscopic and have spacing as little as 2 nanometers (nm) apart. For reference, a human hair is 80,000 to 100,000 nanometers across. With ASML being the sole supplier of a critical machine in the chip manufacturing world, it has a very solid technological monopoly that will be nearly impossible to break. Taiwan Semiconductor's monopoly status is a bit more shaky but still impressive. There are several other chip foundries out there, and many have the same advanced technology available to make the highest-performance chips possible. However, nobody has the scale that TSMC does. During Q2, Taiwan Semiconductor accounted for about 72.5% of revenue in the chip fabrication industry. That's a major size advantage that holds its clients captive, because they couldn't move all of their work to another foundry if they tried, since its competitors wouldn't have the necessary scale. While this advantage could be challenged over time by a rising competitor, there's nobody even close right now. TSMC has great relationships with its clientele, so I doubt its grip on this industry will be broken anytime over the next decade. While I would say ASML's monopoly status is stronger than TSMC's, I can't say the same about their businesses or stocks.

Anyone who has co-signed a loan knows how it works. The borrower pays a rate that reflects the risk, and the co-signer is on the hook if payments stop. Broadcom Inc. (AVGO), one of the world's most valuable chipmakers, just took that seat for Anthropic. CEO Hock Tan spent nearly two months pushing banks to commit more than $40 billion to an Anthropic chip deal, The Wall Street Journal reported. With interest rates rising and AI ventures harder to fund, some lenders felt underpaid for the risk and weighed walking away. Tan held last-minute weekend talks with bank executives and agreed to higher interest rates to keep them in. The deal got done. Bank of America, Citigroup, Morgan Stanley, and Blackstone unveiled the $63 billion package on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026, in a press release. Earlier that day, Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, filed publicly for its IPO under the planned Nasdaq ticker ANT. Also read: Broadcom fought AT&T over VMware: Now a telecom giant is all in In the release, Tan said the deal "validates that there is capital available to finance such growth." I read the weekend scramble differently. The capital was available, but only at a higher price, and only with Broadcom backing the biggest piece. If you own an S&P 500 index fund, you own a slice of Broadcom and the promise it just made. A newly formed company will borrow the money and buy Broadcom's AI chips and networking gear, according to the release. It will lease that equipment to Anthropic, with deliveries expected from 2027. Broadcom's role is where the risk sits. It is providing residual value support, which Reuters called effectively a significant guarantee, for an amount equal to the senior debt. In plain terms, Broadcom shields those lenders from losses if Anthropic defaults, the Journal reported. That senior slice is about $43.5 billion, or roughly 69% of the total, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters. In effect, Broadcom's credit is the safety net under the biggest checks. Blackstone alone provides the committed part of the junior debt beneath it, according to the release. By my math, the remaining $19.5 billion or so carries Anthropic's risk without Broadcom's cushion. To me, that unprotected slice is where lenders priced Anthropic on its own. This isn't Broadcom's first backstop for Anthropic. Apollo Global Management (APO) and Blackstone financed an earlier $35 billion expansion of Anthropic's computing capacity. Broadcom's backstop in that deal was up to $29 billion, Reuters reported, citing a company filing.

Most Read from Bloomberg Apple's Foldable iPhone Duo Draws Early Complaints of the Screen Cracking Lula Wins Record Fourth Term in Surprise Brazil Comeback Finland and Norway Hold 'Frank' Call With Putin on Ukraine Anthropic Files for IPO in Global Race to Raise Cash for AI Mbappé Apologizes for Perceived Mao Insult After China Backlash Bank of America Corp., Citigroup Inc., and Morgan Stanley helped to arrange the $63 billion deal and other banks are expected to submit commitments to join the group in the coming days, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The banks are lending about $42 billion of the amount, as much as half of which is expected to be refinanced in the US high-grade corporate bond market in the first quarter of 2027, they said, asking not to be identified because they're not authorized to speak publicly. The financing is being closely watched across Wall Street and Silicon Valley as bankers and tech executives look for assurance that investors are still eager to lend to artificial intelligence projects. While companies have managed to borrow more than $455 billion across markets globally to fund AI-related spending this year, there are signs that money managers are growing warier of investing in the debt, given how much more could be coming. The transaction is meant to help AI model maker Anthropic pay for equipment including chips for data centers, with Broadcom essentially offering vendor financing. It's set up as a special purpose company, which is borrowing the money to pay for the technology, which it will lease to Anthropic, whose lease payments will in turn pay off the debt, the people said. The $42 billion portion of the debt is senior secured, meaning lenders have a first claim on the assets of the special purpose company, the people said. Broadcom is providing residual value support — a type of financial backstop — for that portion of the debt. Banks have underwritten the senior secured tranche of the $63 billion financing, said one of the people. The bonds that are ultimately sold will probably mature in around five years, and principal on the debt will likely be repaid over the life of the notes. The final size of the bond issuance, and the timing, will depend on market conditions, said the person.

Baird has reiterated its 'outperform' rating on Broadcom Inc (NASDAQ:AVGO, XETRA:1YD) after the chipmaker announced a $63 billion financing arrangement to support artificial intelligence (AI) computing deployments for Anthropic from 2027, highlighting the growth opportunity alongside potential financial risks. The transaction, announced with Bank of America, Citi, Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS) and Blackstone, will fund a special-purpose vehicle (SPV) to purchase Broadcom's custom AI accelerators, known as XPUs, and networking equipment, which will be leased to Anthropic over five years across four sites in four US states. The financing comprises $45 billion of first-lien debt arranged by Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS), and $18 billion of second-lien financing anchored by Blackstone and supported by Anthropic's creditworthiness. The investment bank highlighted Broadcom's residual-value support, which backstops Anthropic's credit and could reach peak exposure of $43 billion near the end of 2027. The potential liability would cover any shortfall between 72.5% of outstanding lease payments and the value of AI racks returned to Broadcom, although management cited safeguards including contractual payments and the ability to sell or redeploy equipment following a default. Broadcom is neither the lender nor the borrower under the arrangement, and its support represents a contingent liability rather than direct borrowing, according to the analysis. The company will receive compensation of a few hundred basis points for providing the backstop, while management expects the underlying computing assets to retain their value. Management said the support currently applies only to Anthropic, although it could consider similar arrangements for OpenAI, but would not extend the structure to large cloud computing companies. Future commitments will be assessed individually, with Anthropic's improving credit profile potentially reducing the required support and allowing standalone financing in 2028. Baird's $630 price target values Broadcom at 18 times its fiscal 2030 earnings-per-share estimate of $35, below the 22-times peer multiple, while citing the company's leading market share in custom AI chips as a supporting factor.

This story was originally published on Utility Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Utility Dive newsletter. The U.S. Department of Energy announced $10.1 billion in loans and loan guarantees to Constellation Energy and Alliant Energy this week, aiming to support 3.7 GW of new capacity from nuclear and other technologies. DOE's Office of Energy Dominance Financing on Tuesday announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion to finance nuclear uprates and modernization across Constellation Energy's fleet in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania. And on Wednesday, EDF, which operated as the Loan Programs Office under the Biden administration, said it closed two loans totaling $5.1 billion to Alliant Energy for new gas-fired power plants, energy storage systems and upgrades to existing generation facilities. EDF manages loan programs with a combined authority exceeding $300 billion, and it is using those funds to bring about a "nuclear renaissance" while addressing issues of energy affordability, according to its strategic plan. Constellation's loan commitment would go toward adding almost 1.1 GW of capacity in the PJM Interconnection and Midcontinent Independent System Operator markets, by boosting capacity and modernizing existing nuclear plants. "Uprates that maximize power generation ... are yet another example of the commonsense energy addition policies the Trump Administration is embracing," U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said in a statement. DOE has set a 5-GW uprate and restart goal for the U.S. nuclear fleet, and Wright said 95% of that capacity has been identified. DOE noted Constellation's planned investments at the Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, LaSalle and Quad Cities nuclear plants in Illinois; Calvert Cliffs in Maryland; and Limerick in Pennsylvania. "EDF's conditional loan commitment also includes an option to finance future uprate projects at additional Constellation facilities," DOE said. However, Constellation "must satisfy certain technical, legal, environmental, and financial conditions before the Department enters into definitive financing documents and funds the loan." The $5.1 billion in loans to Alliant will go to lower electricity costs and bolster grid reliability in Iowa and Wisconsin, DOE said. A filing by Alliant with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Wednesday notes separate loans to two utility subsidiaries: about $1.6 billion for Wisconsin Power & Light and $3.5 billion for Interstate Power and Light.

Constellation Secures $5 Billion DOE Loan Commitment for Nuclear Expansion

Constellation Energy has secured a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to expand nuclear power output across eight existing facilities in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania. The proposed financing would support reactor upgrades and modernizatio...

Constellation Energy has secured a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to expand nuclear power output across eight existing facilities in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania. The proposed financing would support reactor upgrades and modernization projects capable of adding nearly 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of nuclear generating capacity, according to the DOE. The additional electricity would serve the PJM Interconnection and Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) power grids. The financing would cover potential upgrades at six Illinois nuclear plants—Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, LaSalle and Quad Cities—as well as Calvert Cliffs in Maryland and Limerick in Pennsylvania. The announcement comes as U.S. electricity demand accelerates, driven partly by artificial intelligence, data center development and industrial electrification, prompting utilities and technology companies to pursue additional round-the-clock generation capacity. Constellation has already committed billions of dollars to increasing output from its existing nuclear fleet, supported by long-term electricity supply agreements with major technology companies. Recent 20-year agreements with Google and Amazon have helped underpin more than $7 billion in planned investments to add approximately 1,080 megawatts (MW) of nuclear capacity. Under an agreement announced earlier this month, Google will support the addition of 890 MW of nuclear generating capacity through upgrades at 11 reactors across Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. The investment associated with the arrangement exceeds $4.3 billion. Amazon separately signed a 20-year agreement in September supporting a 190-MW expansion at Constellation's Calvert Cliffs nuclear facility in Maryland. A separate agreement with Meta, announced in 2025, supports another 30 MW of nuclear capacity at the Clinton facility in Illinois. The proposed DOE financing could lower borrowing costs and accelerate these types of investments, allowing Constellation to increase electricity production without constructing entirely new nuclear power stations. Unlike new nuclear construction, reactor uprates increase the generating capacity of operational facilities through equipment improvements and efficiency upgrades, potentially delivering additional power on shorter development timelines. The loan commitment also forms part of the DOE's Utility Power Reactor Incremental Scaling Effort (UPRISE), an initiative launched in March 2026 to accelerate nuclear capacity expansion.

Investors might hold Constellation Energy (CEG) as a power company and view power stocks as a calm corner of the market. Constellation has not been calm lately. On October 26, 2026, its shares closed 36.8% below their highest close of the past year. Over the past month they lost 4.1%, while NextEra Energy, Duke Energy and Southern gained between 7.8% and 11.7%. So how far has Constellation stock fallen when the whole market turned, and how long did it stay down? How Far Has Constellation Stock Fallen In Market Shocks? Constellation has usually fallen further than the S&P 500 when the broader market turned. Across the five market shocks Constellation has faced since it began trading in February 2022, the stock fell an average of 21.4%, compared with a 12.8% decline for the index over the same windows. The deepest of those drops occurred during the 2025 US tariff shock, when Constellation lost 47.0% while the S&P 500 lost 19.0%. The stock did not always fall harder, however: during the 2022 inflation shock, it lost 19.0%, slightly less than the 21.1% the S&P 500 lost. The stock has also recovered quickly each time. It returned to its earlier high following all five falls, taking a median of 1.8 months from its low. Even the 2025 decline took only 2.7 months to recover. How Has Constellation's Business Changed In A Year? Constellation is a larger company than it was a year ago, and it has far more debt. Revenue for fiscal Q2 2026, which ended June 30, reached $7.5 billion, up 23.0% from a year earlier. Management said adjusted operating earnings of $2.55 per share were $0.64 higher than a year before, crediting the Calpine acquisition, higher capacity prices and its commercial business. On a reported basis, operating income fell to $580 million from $951 million a year earlier, and GAAP EPS dropped to $1.42 from $2.67, weighed down by unrealized hedge losses and non-cash amortization of Calpine contracts. Over the four quarters ending June 30, the operating margin stood at 14.3%, close to the 13.9% recorded a year before. Total debt climbed to $24.7 billion on June 30, 2026, up from $8.3 billion a year earlier. That debt equals 27.2% of Constellation's market value, compared with 19.4% for the S&P 500. Where Constellation Is Under Pressure Now Management raised its full-year forecast on the August 6, 2026 call, yet also pointed to pressure in Texas, in Illinois and at its nuclear plants. The company now expects adjusted operating earnings of $11.50 to $12.50 per share for fiscal 2026, up from $11 to $12.

Potential financing would help accelerate nuclear uprates that strengthen the grid and deliver more reliable, affordable energy to help meet rising demand BALTIMORE, October 27, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Constellation (Nasdaq: CEG), the nation's largest producer of reliable, emissions-free nuclear energy, today announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion from the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Energy Dominance Financing to support nuclear uprates across select Constellation facilities. The potential funding would help accelerate projects that produce more reliable, around-the-clock power from existing nuclear plants to help meet growing energy demand. The DOE commitment builds on billions of dollars in private-sector investment already supporting Constellation's efforts to increase nuclear output. Recent 20-year agreements with Google and Amazon have incentivized Constellation to invest more than $7 billion to add approximately 1,080 megawatts of nuclear capacity. An agreement announced last year with Meta also supports a 30-megawatt expansion at Clinton Clean Energy Center in Illinois. Together, these agreements demonstrate how large energy users can help enable new, reliable generation that flows to the regional grid and benefits all customers. The conditional loan commitment could lower financing costs and help Constellation deliver additional nuclear capacity at greater scale. Uprates increase electricity production from existing plants, making them one of the fastest and most cost-effective ways to add dependable power without building entirely new generation facilities or transmission corridors. "This is how America wins the race for energy abundance – by pairing private-sector demand and investment with smart federal financing to unlock more power from the nuclear plants we already have," said Joe Dominguez, Constellation chairman, president and CEO. "Our agreements with Google and Amazon demonstrate how long-term customer commitments can incentivize billions of dollars in investment in new, reliable nuclear capacity. This conditional loan commitment can help us move faster and go further, putting more reliable power on the grid, creating and preserving good-paying jobs, strengthening American energy security and helping families and businesses manage energy costs." "The Energy Department is accelerating President Trump's American nuclear renaissance and unlocking the full potential of our nation's nuclear fleet," said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. "Uprates that maximize power generation from our existing nuclear facilities are yet another example of the commonsense energy addition policies the Trump Administration is embracing—ensuring more affordable, reliable, and secure energy for American families and businesses."

Azincourt Energy Advances Labrador Uranium Exploration With New Snegamook Drilling Results

No summary available

Azincourt Energy Corp. (TSX.V:AAZ) (OTC:AZURF) (FSE:A0U0) is continuing to evaluate the resource potential of its Snegamook uranium deposit in Labrador, Canada, after new drilling results identified additional mineralized intervals and helped refine targets for the next phase of exploration. The co...

Azincourt Energy Corp. (TSX.V:AAZ) (OTC:AZURF) (FSE:A0U0) is continuing to evaluate the resource potential of its Snegamook uranium deposit in Labrador, Canada, after new drilling results identified additional mineralized intervals and helped refine targets for the next phase of exploration. The company has completed four diamond drill holes totaling 1,069 meters at Snegamook, part of its Harrier Project in Labrador's Central Mineral Belt. The program is focused on verifying historical uranium discoveries and building the geological data needed to determine whether the deposit can support a maiden mineral resource estimate. Recent results from two holes provided further evidence of uranium mineralization. Hole SN0048 intersected 19 meters grading 0.03% equivalent uranium oxide (eU₃O₈) within a broader 31.6-meter zone of elevated radioactivity. Hole SN0047 returned narrower mineralized intervals, including 0.8 meters grading 0.03% eU₃O₈. The results are helping the company assess the extent and continuity of mineralization identified in earlier drilling. Azincourt's current campaign builds on promising historical results at the property. Previous drilling at hole SN-08-06 returned 0.97% U₃O₈ over 0.5 meters, while a selective check sample collected from the same area in 2025 graded 2.71% U₃O₈ over 10 centimeters. The company cautions that the short sample is not necessarily representative of the grade or width of the broader mineralized interval. The latest program also includes a hole drilled alongside historical hole SN-08-24, which previously intersected 0.05% U₃O₈ over 20 meters. One important caveat is that the latest reported grades are preliminary radiometric estimates derived from downhole gamma measurements, rather than laboratory assay results. Samples have been collected for laboratory testing, with results expected in early 2027. Reported intersection lengths are measured along the drill holes, and true widths have not yet been established. The company now expects to complete approximately 1,800 meters of drilling across six to seven holes during the 2026 program. In addition to testing known mineralization, Azincourt is reviewing historical drill core and plans to work with an independent qualified person to evaluate the available data. The objective is to establish whether the historical results can be verified and whether sufficient geological information exists to support a compliant mineral resource estimate. Snegamook's location adds to its exploration appeal. The deposit sits approximately 1.3 kilometers southeast of the Two Time uranium deposit, where historical work outlined a resource of 6.1 million pounds of U₃O₈. Both areas contain uranium mineralization associated with altered and fractured rock formations, although the geological similarities do not establish the size or economic potential of the Snegamook deposit.

Cameco (NYSE: CCJ), Centrus (NYSE: LEU), and BWX Technologies (NYSE: BWXT) are all linchpins of the nuclear energy market. Cameco is one of the world's largest uranium miners; Centrus is a major uranium enricher, and BWX builds crucial nuclear components. In theory, all three companies should benefit from the nuclear market's recent resurgence -- which was driven by new decarbonization initiatives, safer nuclear technologies, and the expansion of the power-hungry cloud infrastructure and AI markets. But over the past 12 months, Cameco's stock fell 8%, BWX's dipped 7%, and Centrus' plummeted 72%. Let's see why these three nuclear stocks fizzled out -- and which one is the best turnaround play. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Cameco, based in Canada, is the world's second-largest uranium miner after Kazakhstan's Kazatomprom (OTC:NATK.Y). It operates mines in Canada, the U.S., and Kazakhstan. It also owns nearly half of Westinghouse Electric, one of the world's top nuclear plant builders, and Global Laser Enrichment (GLE), its uranium enrichment joint venture with Silex (OTC: SILXY). Cameco still generates most of its revenue from mining. Still, its investments in Westinghouse and GLE could eventually turn it into a "one-stop shop" for mining, converting, and selling enriched uranium. Instead of selling its uranium at spot prices (which would expose it to more volatility), Cameco locks most of its clients into long-term, partly fixed-price contracts. That approach is safer, but it also limits Cameco's exposure to rising uranium prices. Centrus is one of the few U.S. companies licensed to sell low-enriched uranium (LEU), the most common fuel for commercial nuclear reactors. It's also the only public U.S. company authorized to sell high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) for next-gen reactors. Centrus once enriched its own uranium, but it shut down its domestic plants over a decade ago when it became cheaper to import and sell overseas LEU. But in recent years, the sanctions against Russia and the U.S. government's push toward energy independence have driven Centrus to restart its LEU plant in Ohio and begin producing HALEU in the United States. That transformation from a middleman to a first-party producer is squeezing its near-term margins.

The acquisition forms part of Centrus's previously announced multibillion-dollar programme to expand uranium enrichment capacity. The company is investing in manufacturing and production capabilities intended to support the development of additional enrichment infrastructure. Westerman's existing relationship with Centrus means the acquired business already produces components used in the company's centrifuge systems. Secures a key centrifuge component supplier and best-in-class manufacturer with an existing and growing business Diversifies revenue base by expanding Centrus' addressable market with significant adjacent, non-nuclear manufacturing work Drives continued growth for both organizations through commercial and operational synergies and cost savings BETHESDA, Md., Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Centrus Energy Corp. (NYSE: LEU) ("Centrus"), a trusted supplier of nuclear fuel and services, today announced that it has acquired Westerman Holdings, LLC ("Westerman"), one of Centrus' largest and most diversified suppliers, for approximately $116 million, funded through a combination of approximately $95 million cash on hand and $21 million of equity. The transaction is expected to be accretive to adjusted earnings per share in the first year following closing. The acquisition represents a significant milestone for Centrus as it builds supply chain resilience while diversifying its revenue base. Westerman's expertise strengthens and de-risks Centrus' supply chain by securing and bringing in-house its critical manufacturing capabilities. The acquisition simultaneously broadens Centrus' manufacturing platform, customer base, and future revenue opportunities through commercial and operational synergies. The addition of Westerman supports Centrus' previously announced multi-billion-dollar expansion of uranium enrichment capacity. Westerman is an existing manufacturer for centrifuge casings and other major centrifuge components for Centrus. With the acquisition, Centrus intends to secure this key supplier while expanding Westerman's capabilities. Westerman currently services a number of non-nuclear customers across a variety of industries including oil and gas as well as other high-growth industrial sectors, diversifying Centrus' revenue base beyond its core nuclear business. The acquisition is expected to result in lower project costs for Centrus and greater efficiencies with an integrated supply chain. "Westerman is a highly regarded, best-in-class supplier and fabricator for Centrus, the broader nuclear industry, and a number of other sectors," said Amir Vexler, President and CEO of Centrus. "Bringing Westerman in-house demonstrates our commitment to securing our supply chain to support our build-out while adding to our capabilities and expanding our customer base. We are committed to growing and expanding Westerman alongside our enrichment business, and are confident that this transaction will unlock significant value for our shareholders."

Is Centrus Energy the Ultimate Pick-and-Shovel Play on the Nuclear Technology Boom?

Meanwhile, next-generation small modular reactors (SMRs) could begin arriving in the 2030s. Many of these advanced reactors require a specialized ...

Nuclear energy is making a comeback. Governments worldwide are renewing their support, with several committing to triple their nuclear capacity by 2050. Meanwhile, next-generation small modular reactors (SMRs) could begin arriving in the 2030s. Many of these advanced reactors require a specialized fuel that remains in short supply. That's where Centrus Energy (NYSE: LEU) sees its opportunity. The company already supplies low-enriched uranium (LEU) to nuclear power operators, but its biggest growth opportunity could come from high-assay, low-enriched uranium (HALEU). Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Becoming a leading U.S. producer of this next-generation fuel could make Centrus the ultimate pick-and-shovel play on the nuclear technology boom. Here's what investors need to know. Centrus is an important player in the U.S. nuclear fuel supply chain. Currently, the company generates most of its revenue from supplying LEU to utilities operating traditional nuclear reactors in the U.S. and abroad. The company has manufacturing capabilities, but over the last decade, it has sourced this fuel globally, making it an established middleman. However, this is all changing. In 2023, Congress passed the Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act, which blocks the import of natural uranium and LEU produced in Russia or by a Russian entity. Some operators have been given limited waivers to import from Russia, but these waivers are set to expire on Jan. 1, 2028. The restrictions will remain in place until Dec. 31, 2040. Centrus relies heavily on TENEX, a Russian state-owned entity, for its LEU. Over half of the LEU it delivers to customers in 2027 is expected to come from TENEX. Russia holds roughly 43% of global enrichment capacity, so Congress' act creates an urgent need to develop domestic nuclear fuel production. The company is pivoting from being an intermediary to becoming a U.S. producer of these fuels. It is making a multibillion-dollar investment in its Ohio and Tennessee facilities to expand domestic enrichment capacity. In Oak Ridge, Tennessee, management is investing over $560 million to produce thousands of centrifuges. Meanwhile, it's expanding its Piketon, Ohio, centrifuge and enrichment plant to develop LEU and HALEU at scale.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the hot topic on Wall Street and Main Street right now. But for those old enough to remember, the environment may be starting to feel like the dot-com bubble, which burst at the turn of the century. Companies like Oklo (NYSE: OKLO), NuScale Power (NYSE: SMR), and even Constellation Energy (NASDAQ: CEG) all fell around 7% from their highs over the last five days, as of this writing. Bloom Energy (NYSE: BE) is down 13% from its high in that shockingly short period. Meanwhile, ExxonMobil (NYSE: XOM) and Chevron (NYSE: CVX) are hitting all-time highs. There's risk in all of these stocks, but I'd rather own the stocks where the risks are easier to see and understand. That means Exxon and Chevron would be my pick. Here's why. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » The capital spending going into artificial intelligence is massive. AI is just a computer program, so it needs electricity to operate. That should lead to strong demand for power. That's the basic story behind companies like Oklo, NuScale, Bloom Energy, and Constellation Energy. Of the four, Oklo and NuScale are the most speculative. These two companies are attempting to build businesses around small modular nuclear reactors. The opportunity could be huge, but at this point both companies are losing money and haven't yet proven their technologies are financially viable. Only the most aggressive investors should be considering them. Bloom Energy and Constellation Energy have established and profitable businesses. Bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells that provide off-grid power to AI data centers. Constellation Energy is an independent power producer selling power to the tech companies building out their AI operations. Bloom is the more aggressive option, as investors have priced a lot of good news into the stock. Even after a material pullback, the price-to-earnings ratio is still over 100x. Constellation Energy is probably the best positioned to weather an AI pullback, given the long-term contracts it signs, but irrational investors tend to throw the baby out with the bathwater when things turn south. If the AI bubble bursts, all of these stocks are likely to be hard hit, and the pullback over the last week is a sign of the all-or-nothing approach investors often take with new technologies.

This too shall pass, with oil prices likely to eventually fall, just like they have every other time they have spiked higher. The bigger story in energy is the shifting dynamics of demand taking shape. And that is why you should probably stick with industry-leading energy businesses like ExxonMobil (NYSE: XOM), TotalEnergies (NYSE: TTE), and Enterprise Products Partners (NYSE: EPD). Here's a look at each one. Exxon is one of the world's largest energy companies, with a portfolio spread across the upstream (production), midstream (pipeline), and downstream (chemicals and refining) sectors. Its 0.16x debt-to-equity ratio is better than any of its closest peers. And it has rewarded investors with 43 consecutive annual dividend increases. Conservatively managed, Exxon is built to survive the entire energy cycle. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » This is important to keep in mind today because when oil prices are high, investors often forget that they can also go down. If you want to buy and hold an energy stock, Exxon is a solid option. And you get to collect a well-above-market 2.3% dividend yield, as well. However, this is really about owning a company that has the scale to handle whatever gets thrown at it. One of the things happening right now is a shift away from dirtier carbon fuels and toward cleaner power sources, such as electricity and renewable power. Exxon hasn't pivoted yet, but when the time comes, it should be able to do so relatively easily. TotalEnergies isn't waiting; it is starting to build a division around electricity and clean energy right now. In 2025, the company's integrated power business accounted for nearly 12% of adjusted net operating income. Through the first half of 2026, that was down to around 8%, but only because the company's production and refining operations have benefited from the turmoil in the energy sector. If you are worried about the long-term trend toward clean energy and aren't willing to wait for Exxon to pivot, TotalEnergies could be the integrated energy major you want to buy. You get the benefit of oil exposure today, a business diversified across the entire energy value chain, and a head start on the clean energy transition that, basically, no other integrated energy company is currently offering. And all of that comes with a 4.4% dividend yield (U.S. investors have to pay French taxes on the dividend, but some of that can be claimed back come April 15).

Exxon just showed why gas prices didn't fall with oil

No summary available

There's a quiet rule in household budgeting. The bills that hurt most are the ones you can't negotiate. You can shop around for car insurance and switch phone plans. You can't haggle at the pump. For most of 2026, that rule has been expensive. Last month was the priciest September on record for ga...

There's a quiet rule in household budgeting. The bills that hurt most are the ones you can't negotiate. You can shop around for car insurance and switch phone plans. You can't haggle at the pump. For most of 2026, that rule has been expensive. Last month was the priciest September on record for gasoline, with the monthly national average landing at $4.33 a gallon, 50 cents above the prior September high, according to AAA. By Oct. 17, the national average was still about $4.31 a gallon, AAA noted. Here's the part that should really bother you. Crude oil, the raw ingredient in every gallon, got cheaper over the summer. The average Brent closing price fell about 5.6% in the third quarter from the second, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters. So where did that relief go? ExxonMobil just answered the question in a regulatory filing. The company said on Oct. 16 that higher refining margins could add $4.5 billion to third-quarter earnings in its Energy Products segment compared with the second quarter, according to its Form 8-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Exxon plans to post full third-quarter results at about 5:30 a.m. Central time on Oct. 30. The 8-K isn't an earnings forecast, and Exxon says so plainly. It's a list of market and planned factors management expects to move results from one quarter to the next. The numbers still tell a clear story. Here's how the biggest pieces stack up against the second quarter, according to the filing: Refining margins in Energy Products: +$4.5 billion Specialty Products margins: +$500 million Chemical Products margins: -$600 million Lower crude and liquids prices in Upstream: -$1.3 billion Natural gas prices: +$300 million Lighter scheduled maintenance: +$200 million Estimated timing effects: -$2.5 billion, which Exxon strips out of adjusted earnings In my read of that table, the oil-pumping side of Exxon lost $1.3 billion to cheaper crude, while the fuel-making side picked up more than three times that amount. Analysts expect Exxon's third-quarter refining earnings to land near $7.8 billion, which would be a company record, according to Bloomberg. BMO Capital Markets analyst Phillip Jungwirth went higher, writing that refining adjusted net income could reach $8.5 billion, Reuters reported. Either figure would roughly double the $4.1 billion the refining business earned in the second quarter. A refining margin is the gap between what a refiner pays for crude and what it gets for gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. When that gap widens, refiners win, and drivers cover the difference.

Can Industrial Heat Demand Drive Growth for NuScale Stock?

NuScale Power Corporation SMR is exploring industrial heat as a use for its small modular reactors. Factories need heat to refine crude oil, produce chemicals and manufacture fertilizers, with much of that energy coming from fossil fuels. According to a U.S. Department of Energy analysis cited by Nu...

NuScale Power Corporation SMR is exploring industrial heat as a use for its small modular reactors. Factories need heat to refine crude oil, produce chemicals and manufacture fertilizers, with much of that energy coming from fossil fuels. According to a U.S. Department of Energy analysis cited by NuScale, process heating accounted for 51% of manufacturing energy use in 2018. NuScale says a plant with 12 Power Modules could supply 3 gigawatts of thermal energy as superheated steam. This could give industrial customers another way to meet their heat needs while reducing emissions. Industrial facilities need steam at specific temperatures and pressures, making it difficult to replace conventional boilers. NuScale has been studying how its reactors could meet those requirements. In a 2025 assessment published with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, several proposed systems were found capable of serving a large chemical facility while potentially cutting carbon dioxide emissions by 80% to 90%. NuScale is also working with Ebara Elliott Energy on a high-temperature steam compressor. The planned system would use equipment to raise reactor-supplied steam to 500°C or more, making it suitable for additional industrial uses. These projects could open another market for NuScale, although commercial adoption remains uncertain. Its reactor design supports an emergency planning zone at the plant boundary, allowing installations closer to factories and reducing heat lost during transport. The company has studied ways to supply electricity and steam for hydrogen and ammonia production. However, these studies do not amount to industrial sales. NuScale must demonstrate its systems at commercial scale, secure customers and arrange financing before process heat can become a revenue source. Successful projects could improve the business outlook for SMR stock. NuScale is not alone in exploring nuclear energy for industrial heat applications. Other advanced nuclear developers are also working on smaller reactor designs that could supply both electricity and heat to industrial facilities. As industries look for ways to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels, demand for such technologies could increase, creating new business opportunities while intensifying competition in the nuclear energy market. NANO Nuclear Energy NNE is targeting applications where reliable, high-temperature energy can support power-intensive industrial operations. NANO Nuclear Energy says its KRONOS MMR uses high-temperature gas-cooled reactor technology and is designed for deployment across data centers, industrial and defense-related customers. Its compact, modular architecture and use of TRISO fuel could support co-located or off-grid applications. NANO Nuclear Energy is also building partnerships to support future commercial deployment.

Almost exactly a year ago, on Oct. 15, 2025, shares of NuScale Power (NYSE:SMR) finished the day at a record $53.43. On Monday, they ended at $5.69. That's around 89% lower, and it's the stock's lowest close since May 2024. Shares are down about 60% for 2026, including a 26% fall from their Oct. 7 close at $7.67. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » At this price, most of what a buyer pays for every share is cash. To me, that's the biggest shift in this stock over the last year. A stock trading so close to its cash can look like a value stock. But it isn't necessarily cheap when the company keeps selling new shares to refill the cash. Image source: Getty Images. As of June 30, 2026, NuScale's cash, cash equivalents, and short- and long-term investments totaled $1.9 billion, and it has no debt. Divided by the roughly 430 million Class A and Class B shares outstanding on June 30, that's about $4.41 per share. That means cash and investments equal around 78% of Monday's closing price. And with no net income to measure the stock against, that cash is arguably the best gauge. NuScale's filing for its newest stock offering put its net tangible book value (assets minus liabilities, not counting intangibles like goodwill) even higher, at $4.63 per share at the end of June. So a buyer at $5.69 pays a bit over $1 per share (about $450 million in all) for everything else -- the reactor technology, the engineering team, and whatever orders eventually come through partner ENTRA1 Energy. NuScale has almost no revenue yet, just $75,000 for the second quarter of 2026, down from $8.1 million a year before. Still, the company doesn't burn cash very fast. Its operating activities used $314.7 million in the first quarter of 2026. But $259.9 million of that was one payment to ENTRA1. Take that payment out, and the company used around $55 million of cash over those three months, then about $58 million from April through June. That rate is accelerating, though, up from about $33 million in the second quarter of 2025. Losses are rising, too. NuScale's operating loss was $64 million in the second quarter -- 49% higher than a year before and over the first quarter's $58 million. That said, at roughly $230 million a year, $1.9 billion could fund several years of spending. Cash likely isn't NuScale's short-term issue.
