Nuclear energy stocks are becoming closely tied to the data center build-out. Alphabet's Google recently signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation Energy, the U.S.'s largest nuclear operator, to support its growing power needs. After its Oct. 6 announcement, Constellation's stock soared 12%, and other nuclear energy stocks followed suit. One intriguing stock in the space is NuScale Power (NYSE: SMR), an early-stage developer of small modular reactors (SMRs). As hyperscale data center operators search for dependable, carbon-free electricity, NuScale could offer investors another way to capitalize on the nuclear energy revival. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » The early-stage company trades below $6 per share and is largely story-driven, but one key catalyst could send the stock soaring. NuScale's Power Modules are factory-built SMRs that are based on light-water reactor technology. Each module produces 77 MWe (megawatt-electric) of power and can be deployed in multiunit arrays to provide up to 924 MWe, enough to power 700,000 homes or heavy-duty infrastructure such as data centers or industrial plants. The stock surged last year as data center investments ramped up and the Department of Energy took steps to boost the nuclear energy industry. As part of these efforts, the U.S. has an aggressive goal of quadrupling nuclear energy capacity by 2050 and is building traditional power plants while accelerating the development of microreactor and SMR technology. Over the past year, the stock has plunged. After peaking at around $57 per share, NuScale is down over 90%. Several factors are driving the decline, including weakness in nuclear energy stocks, Fluor (an early investor in NuScale) exiting its stake, and a lack of further commitments for its technology. NuScale has one project in Romania, but it needs more in its pipeline to gain real traction. One deal that could send the stock soaring is with the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA). NuScale is working with ENTRA1 to develop power plants, and on Sept. 2, 2025, ENTRA1 signed a non-binding agreement with the TVA for up to 6 gigawatts (GW) of power across its service region. The 6 GW project would be the largest SMR deployment in the U.S. and would require deploying up to 72 NuScale Power Modules. A deal would transform NuScale's long-term outlook.

Most Of NuScale Power's Market Value Is Cash Buyers of the stock acquire a large cash reserve first and a nuclear developer second. Subtracting those liquid assets reveals the price of the operating business itself, a metric investors refer to as enterprise value. For NuScale, that calculation lands at about $750 million. This represents the price paid for the reactor operations. That cash reserve remains in flux. Issuing new stock raises cash, yet it leaves each existing share representing a smaller piece of the company. What Does NuScale Power's Business Bring In Today? The broader S&P 500 traded at 3.1 times over the same period. That elevated multiple exists because NuScale sales nearly vanished, rather than because investors bid up the shares. That installation would deploy six NuScale power modules at a former coal plant site.

Owning it has been a roller-coaster ride, with five drawdowns of 50% or more over that span. The current drawdown is the worst of them, at roughly 85%. That said, there's a clear event that could prompt investors to rethink their views of NuScale Power. The interesting thing about NuScale Power's huge price swings is that they aren't really driven by its business. That 85% decline didn't happen because of some terrible corporate disaster; it happened because investors got overly enthusiastic about nuclear power stocks, and then moved on to other things. NuScale Power, a nuclear power start-up at the leading edge of nuclear technology, simply went along for the ride. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » The technology NuScale Power is working on is small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs). It could be a game changer for the nuclear industry, as factory-built SMRs could be less costly, safer, and easier to place near where they are needed than current large-scale reactors. But the hard truth is that NuScale Power hasn't even built its first commercial SMR yet. It has an approved reactor design, which is a very big deal, but it still needs to find the first customer willing to sign on the dotted line. To the company's credit, it is working hard to ink that first sale. It has been working with the Romanian power company RoPower for quite some time and is seeing material success. RoPower has approved a project that would use six NuScale Power SMRs. But RoPower still needs to nail down project financing, so there's no agreement yet. NuScale Power is also working closely with ENTRA1 Energy and the Tennessee Valley Authority in hopes of being part of what could be "the largest nuclear power deployment program in U.S. history." But, like RoPower, there is still no deal yet. So, what the market is likely waiting for is NuScale Power's first SMR sale. That could be the event that pushes the stock back toward $20. However, it is important to remember that a signed contract is really just the start of the next stage of the company's development. Once it has that contract, it still needs to prove it can build an SMR and that the SMRs it builds are reliable and safe. In other words, NuScale Power is a high-risk start-up, and that isn't likely to change for quite some time.

NuScale Power (NYSE:SMR) says it holds the only design certification the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has given a small modular reactor. Its newer US460 design, based on bigger 77-megawatt modules, also earned the agency's standard design approval in May 2025. But the first commercial small modular reactor the NRC has approved for construction isn't a NuScale design. On Sept. 29, the regulator granted a permit for the Tennessee Valley Authority to build a 300-megawatt BWRX-300 reactor from GE Vernova (NYSE:GEV) on TVA's Clinch River site in Tennessee. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » NuScale shares trade near $8 as I write, down about 86% from the $57.42 they hit a year ago. And the permit came under three weeks after UBS cut the growth stock to sell, arguing rivals were moving into construction but NuScale had no firm customer commitments. I wouldn't buy or sell a stock over a rating change. But it's worth comparing how TVA won its permit to where NuScale's own customers are. Image source: The Motley Fool. The NRC officially started reviewing TVA's application in July 2025 and finished in 14 months, four months ahead of schedule. And TVA already had an early site permit for Clinch River, granted in 2019. The GE Vernova design is moving in Canada, too. Ontario Power Generation got a license to construct the first BWRX-300 in April 2025, and nuclear construction is now underway at its Darlington site. NRC records for NuScale look different. The agency lists NuScale in pre-application work for future combined license applications (the filing a utility submits to build and operate a plant) that would reference the US460 design. When it approved the design, the NRC said that anyone wanting to use it would still need to apply to build and operate a reactor. None has done that yet. Everything goes through ENTRA1 Energy, NuScale's exclusive commercialization partner. In September 2025, ENTRA1 and TVA signed a non-binding agreement for up to 6 gigawatts of capacity from NuScale's power modules, billed partly as power for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. As of NuScale's second-quarter report in August, ENTRA1 was still working toward a definitive power purchase agreement with TVA. The license application itself waits for that agreement. On NuScale's second-quarter earnings call, CEO John Hopkins said one of the first steps once power purchase agreements are in place would be starting the license application with the customer. He added that around 60% of the application work done for a scrapped Utah project could be reused.

It's one of the biggest building booms in recent history. Data centers are energy-intensive, and because demand in many parts of the world has flatlined in recent years, current grid infrastructure isn't suited to handle a multiyear ramp-up in demand. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. According to research by Goldman Sachs: "Nuclear power will be a key part of a suite of new energy infrastructure built to meet surging data-center power demand driven by artificial intelligence. In the U.S. alone, big tech companies have signed new contracts for more than 10 GW of possible new nuclear capacity in the last year, and Goldman Sachs Research sees potential for three plants to be brought on line by 2030." Nuclear power is an ideal solution, given that it can deliver a huge amount of reliable, low-carbon electricity. But there's a problem: Nuclear power plants often cost billions of dollars to build, with construction sometimes stretching for a decade or more. AI companies need new power sources fast, and they want to avoid diverting capital away from building more computing infrastructure. Experts increasingly view small modular reactors, or SMRs, as solutions to this challenge. Bank of America says, "[N]ew advancements in technology may now make the tipping point in sight for small modular reactors to reshape nuclear energy supply chains over the next decade." The bank sees five major advantages for SMRs: lower up-front costs, improved safety, lower carbon emissions, smaller footprints, and the ability to modularize. Want to gain exposure to SMRs? Dozens of companies are pursuing the technology worldwide, but most are either privately held or part of a larger, more diversified conglomerate. Fortunately, three stocks with meaningful SMR exposure are currently publicly traded. Oklo (NYSE: OKLO) is betting that AI providers will want to control their means of energy production. The company intends to finance and construct their own plants near data center infrastructure, selling the energy production to AI companies through long-term power purchase agreements.

That's actually not so bad when you compare it to the $1.1 billion in cash the company has, suggesting NuScale could muddle along for another four years before cash would become a problem. That said, NuScale just set up a new at-the-money stock program to raise as much as $750 million in new capital. It doesn't need to sell that stock right now, but it is clearly preparing to do so and likely for good reason. At the moment, it is basically in a holding pattern as it waits to sign its first official sale. When that happens, it needs to start manufacturing its SMRs, which will be a costly effort. In other words, investors have two different issues to watch. NuScale appears to have plenty of cash on hand to support the business as it works toward its first sale. But once it makes its first sale, spending will likely accelerate quickly, and its cash burn will increase materially. Even there, however, the company appears prepared, as evidenced by the at-the-money stock program it has implemented. Essentially, even though you should continue to watch the company's cash hoard, it looks like NuScale is positioned fairly well from a cash perspective right now.

It also owns nearly half of Westinghouse Electric, one of the world's top nuclear plant builders, and Global Laser Enrichment (GLE), its uranium enrichment joint venture with Silex (OTC: SILXY). Cameco still generates most of its revenue from mining. Still, its investments in Westinghouse and GLE could eventually turn it into a "one-stop shop" for mining, converting, and selling enriched uranium. That approach is safer, but it also limits Cameco's exposure to rising uranium prices. Centrus is one of the few U.S. companies licensed to sell low-enriched uranium (LEU), the most common fuel for commercial nuclear reactors. It's also the only public U.S. company authorized to sell high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) for next-gen reactors. Centrus once enriched its own uranium, but it shut down its domestic plants over a decade ago when it became cheaper to import and sell overseas LEU. But in recent years, the sanctions against Russia and the U.S. government's push toward energy independence have driven Centrus to restart its LEU plant in Ohio and begin producing HALEU in the United States. That transformation from a middleman to a first-party producer is squeezing its near-term margins.

Shares closed at $85.18 on October 2. How quickly Cameco's contract book catches up to that price decides how much of it reaches earnings. The lag is built into how Cameco sells. President and COO Grant Isaac said on the July 31 earnings call that market-related contracts "don't reference the long-term price" and instead carry floors and ceilings, adding that "it's not unusual to see market-related contracts now where floor prices are in the high 70s escalated and where ceiling prices are 160 escalated." Those floors sit above the Q2 realized price, and Isaac noted "we've never been at this kind of uranium price on the front end of a uranium contracting cycle." Repricing reaches the book slowly. Cameco has contracts for average annual deliveries of over 28 million pounds through 2030, with commitments above that average in 2026 through 2028 and below it in 2029 and 2030, leaving more room to sign new volume later in the decade. CEO Tim Gitzel said Cameco is "not prepared to dilute the value of our assets by committing supply into contracts that do not appropriately reflect the durability of market fundamentals." The risk is competition for that volume. Isaac said: "There still seems to be some in the market willing to try to discount floors and ceilings in order to win business." Q2 showed how much of the price gain costs can absorb. Higher US$ realized prices added C$104 million to uranium gross profit versus Q2 2025, but currency took back C$19 million and higher costs C$103 million, as Cameco's produced and purchased cost rose 36% to C$62.21 per pound, including 2.8 million pounds bought at C$91.40. Adjusted EPS of C$0.18 also missed the C$0.38 estimate. Isaac pointed downstream for a leading signal, saying "you generally buy nuclear fuel backwards," starting with fabrication, then enrichment and conversion, then uranium. Why Elon Musk's Latest Trillion-Dollar Forecast for SpaceX Is One That Investors Should Take With a Grain of Salt

No summary available

Investors expect big things from Space Exploration Technologies Corp (NASDAQ:SPCX), and CEO Elon Musk often pumps up the company's growth prospects, both in the long run and in the short term. Between telecom, artificial intelligence (AI), and space, there is an abundance of growth potential for the...

Investors expect big things from Space Exploration Technologies Corp (NASDAQ:SPCX), and CEO Elon Musk often pumps up the company's growth prospects, both in the long run and in the short term. Between telecom, artificial intelligence (AI), and space, there is an abundance of growth potential for the business. And that's a key reason many investors don't balk at buying the stock despite its high valuation -- SpaceX has a market cap of around $2 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies in the world. While there's no shortage of excitement around its opportunities, Musk's latest forecast for the business stood out for multiple reasons. Not only did it call for $1 trillion in revenue at an earlier time frame than in the past, but the range was also incredibly wide; investors should take it with a grain of salt. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Image source: Getty Images. SpaceX reported earnings last week, and much of the focus was on what lies ahead for business. This is, after all, a company whose valuation is more closely tied to future expectations rather than what it has accomplished thus far. With grand ambitions related to space travel, AI, and disrupting the telecom sector, investors are always eager to hear about SpaceX's future. Previously, Musk said that SpaceX could hit $1 trillion in revenue by 2030. Now, however, Musk has suggested that the business could hit that milestone even earlier, saying on the company's recent earnings call that its annual recurring revenue could get to $1 trillion by the end of next year. But that's the top end of the range. His full range was $500 billion to $1 trillion. It's little wonder that CFO Bret Johnsen reportedly laughed when hearing that outlook, since that doesn't amount to much of a forecast at all. The broad range is what's troubling, as it implies a great deal of uncertainty, as if Musk threw out the number to suggest it is possible to get there in the near term. But given the significant range, investors shouldn't take it too seriously. While SpaceX has a bright future and a ton of growth potential, investors who buy the stock shouldn't ignore its high valuation. At around $2 trillion in market cap, it might seem like a cheap buy if its revenue does hit $1 trillion within a few years, but a lot would have to go right for that to happen. The company generated $14.6 billion in revenue during its most recent quarter, putting it at an annual run rate of around $58 billion -- nowhere near $1 trillion.

Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) just upped the ante in the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure race, planning to increase its computing capacity by about 10 gigawatts next year, with a moonshot goal of boosting it by 20 gigawatts. That's a huge amount of spending, with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), SK Hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY), Vertiv (NYSE: VRT), Amphenol (NYSE: APH), and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM) among the biggest beneficiaries. Let's look at how each of these artificial intelligence stocks could benefit. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Nvidia will be the biggest beneficiary of SpaceX's AI infrastructure spree. SpaceX will build its data centers exclusively using Nvidia's Vera Rubin architecture, which means the semiconductor company will supply virtually all the chips and networking for this enormous build-out. Nvidia gets roughly $40 billion per gigawatt from Vera Rubin, so this could be a $400 billion-plus revenue boost if it doesn't take capacity away from other customers. The current analyst average estimate is for Nvidia to generate roughly $412 billion in revenue this fiscal year (ending January 2027), so this would be a gigantic one-year order from SpaceX. Without high bandwidth memory (HBM), Nvidia's ultra-expensive graphics processing units (GPUs) can't deliver their full potential in handling AI workloads. As such, HBM has become essential to the AI build-out. However, HBM is currently in short supply, and memory companies' ability to quickly increase supply is limited by their capacity to purchase more extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, which are used to make the critical components in both HBM and advanced logic chips, such as GPUs and central processing units (CPUs). This has resulted in a major supply-demand imbalance across the entire memory market, leading to skyrocketing prices across the board. SK Hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY), meanwhile, looks to be the memory company most likely to benefit from SpaceX's increased AI infrastructure spending, as it is the HBM leader with more than 50% market share and a close relationship with Nvidia. The two companies already have a $500 billion long-term supply deal in place, and SpaceX's spending will only increase demand for HBM and memory in an already constrained market.

This points to an important part of the SpaceX business: The developments of one unit benefit the other businesses, suggesting that as SpaceX progresses, we may see increasing efficiency. The ability to transport equipment to space rather than relying on others would offer huge cost savings and control over the timing of launches. And this could be applied to both the connectivity and SI businesses -- it's important to remember that SpaceX has a goal of putting data centers in space.
